title: 伊索寓言
author: Aesop 伊索
description: 《The Aesop for Children》(1919):Milo Winter 編選嘅 147 則伊索寓言,語言簡單、故事短小,最適合初學者閱讀。

chapters.title: The Wolf and the Kid 狼與小山羊

passages.original: CH There was once a little Kid whose growing horns made him think he was a grown-up Billy Goat and able to take care of himself. So one evening when the flock started home from the pasture and his mother called, the Kid paid no heed and kept right on nibbling the tender grass. A little later when he lifted his head, the flock was gone.
passages.vernacular: 從前有一隻小山羊,頭上嘅角漸漸長出嚟,佢就以為自己係一隻長大咗嘅公山羊,可以照顧自己喇。於是有一天傍晚,羊群從牧場往家走,佢母親喺叫佢,小山羊卻不理不睬,仍然繼續啃住嫩草。過咗一會兒,佢抬起頭嚟,羊群已經唔見喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 從前有一隻小山羊,頭上的角漸漸長出來,他就以為自己是一隻長大了的公山羊,可以照顧自己了。於是有一天傍晚,羊群從牧場往家走,他母親在叫他,小山羊卻不理不睬,仍然繼續啃著嫩草。過了一會兒,他抬起頭來,羊群已經不見了。

passages.original: He was all alone. The sun was sinking. Long shadows came creeping over the ground. A chilly little wind came creeping with them making scary noises in the grass. The Kid shivered as he thought of the terrible Wolf. Then he started wildly over the field, bleating for his mother. But not half-way, near a clump of trees, there was the Wolf!
passages.vernacular: 佢孤零零一個。太陽正在下沉。長長嘅影子爬過地面。一陣冰涼嘅小風跟住爬嚟,喺草叢裡發出嚇人嘅聲響。小山羊一想到嗰可怕嘅狼,就渾身發抖。然後佢發瘋似嘅跑過田野,咩咩地叫住找媽媽。不過仲冇跑到一半,喺一叢樹木旁邊,狼就喺嗰度!
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他孤零零一個。太陽正在下沉。長長的影子爬過地面。一陣冰涼的小風跟著爬來,在草叢裡發出嚇人的聲響。小山羊一想到那可怕的狼,就渾身發抖。然後他發瘋似的跑過田野,咩咩地叫著找媽媽。可是還沒跑到一半,在一叢樹木旁邊,狼就在那裡!

passages.original: The Kid knew there was little hope for him.
passages.vernacular: 小山羊知道自己冇乜嘢指望喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 小山羊知道自己沒什麼指望了。

passages.original: "Please, Mr. Wolf," he said trembling, "I know you are going to eat me. But first please pipe me a tune, for I want to dance and be merry as long as I can."
passages.vernacular: 「狼先生,請你,」佢發住抖講,「我知道你要食掉我。但係請你先畀我吹一支曲子,因為我想盡量跳舞、玩得開心。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「狼先生,請你,」他發著抖說,「我知道你要吃掉我。但是請你先給我吹一支曲子,因為我想盡量跳舞、玩得開心。」

passages.original: The Wolf liked the idea of a little music before eating, so he struck up a merry tune and the Kid leaped and frisked gaily.
passages.vernacular: 狼覺得食之前有點音樂係個好主意,就吹起一支歡快嘅曲子,小山羊蹦跳住,快活地嬉戲。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 狼覺得吃之前有點音樂是個好主意,就吹起一支歡快的曲子,小山羊蹦跳著,快活地嬉戲。

passages.original: Meanwhile, the flock was moving slowly homeward. In the still evening air the Wolf's piping carried far. The Shepherd Dogs pricked up their ears. They recognized the song the Wolf sings before a feast, and in a moment they were racing back to the pasture. The Wolf's song ended suddenly, and as he ran, with the Dogs at his heels, he called himself a fool for turning piper to please a Kid, when he should have stuck to his butcher's trade.
passages.vernacular: 呢陣候,羊群正慢慢往家走。喺寧靜嘅傍晚空氣裡,狼嘅笛聲傳得好遠。牧羊犬豎起咗耳朵。牠哋認出呢個係狼喺飽餐之前唱嘅歌,轉眼間就飛奔回牧場。狼嘅歌聲突然停喇,佢一邊逃跑,一邊被狗追喺腳後跟,罵自己係傻瓜,為了討好一隻小山羊去當吹笛手,本來應該老老實實幹佢屠夫嘅本行。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 這時候,羊群正慢慢往家走。在寧靜的傍晚空氣裡,狼的笛聲傳得很遠。牧羊犬豎起了耳朵。牠們認出這是狼在飽餐之前唱的歌,轉眼間就飛奔回牧場。狼的歌聲突然停了,他一邊逃跑,一邊被狗追在腳後跟,罵自己是傻瓜,為了討好一隻小山羊去當吹笛手,本來應該老老實實幹他屠夫的本行。

passages.original: Do not let anything turn you from your purpose.
passages.vernacular: 唔好讓任何事物使你偏離你嘅目標。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不要讓任何事物使你偏離你的目標。

chapters.title: The Tortoise and the Ducks 烏龜與鴨子

passages.original: CH The Tortoise, you know, carries his house on his back. No matter how hard he tries, he cannot leave home. They say that Jupiter punished him so, because he was such a lazy stay-at-home that he would not go to Jupiter's wedding, even when especially invited.
passages.vernacular: 你知道,烏龜係把房子背喺背上嘅。不管佢點樣努力,佢都離不開家。據講係朱比特咁樣懲罰佢嘅,因為佢係個懶惰嘅宅喺家裡嘅傢伙,連朱比特嘅婚禮都唔肯去,即使特別邀請咗佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 你知道,烏龜是把房子背在背上的。不管他怎樣努力,他都離不開家。據說是朱比特這樣懲罰他的,因為他是個懶惰的宅在家裡的傢伙,連朱比特的婚禮都不肯去,即使特別邀請了他。

passages.original: After many years, Tortoise began to wish he had gone to that wedding. When he saw how gaily the birds flew about and how the Hare and the Chipmunk and all the other animals ran nimbly by, always eager to see everything there was to be seen, the Tortoise felt very sad and discontented. He wanted to see the world too, and there he was with a house on his back and little short legs that could hardly drag him along.
passages.vernacular: 過咗好多年,烏龜開始後悔當初冇去嗰場婚禮。佢睇見鳥兒飛得幾咁歡暢,兔子、花栗鼠同所有別嘅動物輕快地跑過,總是急住要睇遍所有能睇嘅嘢,烏龜覺得好傷心同不滿。佢都想睇睇世界,可佢背上背住一座房子,腿又短又小,幾乎拖不動身體。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 過了很多年,烏龜開始後悔當初沒去那場婚禮。他看見鳥兒飛得多麼歡暢,兔子、花栗鼠和所有別的動物輕快地跑過,總是急著要看遍所有能看的東西,烏龜覺得非常傷心和不滿。他也想看看世界,可他背上背著一座房子,腿又短又小,幾乎拖不動身體。

passages.original: One day he met a pair of Ducks and told them all his trouble.
passages.vernacular: 有一天,佢遇見一對鴨子,把佢所有嘅煩惱告訴咗牠哋。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 有一天,他遇見一對鴨子,把他所有的煩惱告訴了牠們。

passages.original: "We can help you to see the world," said the Ducks. "Take hold of this stick with your teeth and we will carry you far up in the air where you can see the whole countryside. But keep quiet or you will be sorry."
passages.vernacular: 「我哋可以幫你睇睇世界,」鴨子講。「用牙齒咬住呢根棍子,我哋把你帶到高高嘅空中,你就能睇見整片鄉野。但係要保持安靜,否則你會後悔嘅。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我們可以幫你看看世界,」鴨子說。「用牙齒咬住這根棍子,我們把你帶到高高的空中,你就能看見整片鄉野。但是要保持安靜,否則你會後悔的。」

passages.original: The Tortoise was very glad indeed. He seized the stick firmly with his teeth, the two Ducks took hold of it one at each end, and away they sailed up toward the clouds.
passages.vernacular: 烏龜真嘅好高興。佢用牙齒牢牢咬住棍子,兩隻鴨子一邊一個銜住棍子嘅兩端,就朝住雲端飛去。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 烏龜真的非常高興。他用牙齒牢牢咬住棍子,兩隻鴨子一邊一個銜住棍子的兩端,就朝著雲端飛去。

passages.original: Just then a Crow flew by. He was very much astonished at the strange sight and cried:
passages.vernacular: 呢陣一隻烏鴉飛過。佢對呢奇怪嘅景象大為驚訝,喊道:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 這時一隻烏鴉飛過。他對這奇怪的景象大為驚訝,喊道:

passages.original: "This must surely be the King of Tortoises!"
passages.vernacular: 「呢一定係烏龜之王!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這一定是烏龜之王!」

passages.original: "Why certainly----" began the Tortoise.
passages.vernacular: 「嗰仲用講——」烏龜開口講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「那還用說——」烏龜開口說。

passages.original: But as he opened his mouth to say these foolish words he lost his hold on the stick, and down he fell to the ground, where he was dashed to pieces on a rock.
passages.vernacular: 不過佢一張嘴要講呢句愚蠢嘅話,就鬆開咗棍子,掉到地上,喺一塊岩石上摔得粉碎。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 可是他一張嘴要說這句愚蠢的話,就鬆開了棍子,掉到地上,在一塊岩石上摔得粉碎。

passages.original: Foolish curiosity and vanity often lead to misfortune.
passages.vernacular: 愚蠢嘅好奇心同虛榮心常常招致不幸。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 愚蠢的好奇心和虛榮心常常招致不幸。

chapters.title: The Young Crab and His Mother 小螃蟹與媽媽

passages.original: CH "Why in the world do you walk sideways like that?" said a Mother Crab to her son. "You should always walk straight forward with your toes turned out."
passages.vernacular: 「你到底點解要咁樣橫住走路?」一隻母螃蟹對佢嘅兒子講。「你應該總是直直往前走,腳趾向外。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你到底為什麼要這樣橫著走路?」一隻母螃蟹對她的兒子說。「你應該總是直直往前走,腳趾向外。」

passages.original: "Show me how to walk, mother dear," answered the little Crab obediently, "I want to learn."
passages.vernacular: 「媽媽,請你教我點樣走吧,」小螃蟹乖乖地回答,「我想學。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「媽媽,請你教我怎樣走吧,」小螃蟹乖乖地回答,「我想學。」

passages.original: So the old Crab tried and tried to walk straight forward. But she could walk sideways only, like her son. And when she wanted to turn her toes out she tripped and fell on her nose.
passages.vernacular: 於是老螃蟹試咗又試,想要直直往前走。不過佢只能像佢兒子嗰樣橫住走。而且當佢想把腳趾向外轉嘅時候,就絆咗一跤,摔得鼻子住地。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 於是老螃蟹試了又試,想要直直往前走。可是她只能像她兒子那樣橫著走。而且當她想把腳趾向外轉的時候,就絆了一跤,摔得鼻子著地。

passages.original: Do not tell others how to act unless you can set a good example.
passages.vernacular: 除非你能樹立好榜樣,否則唔好告訴別人該點做。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 除非你能樹立好榜樣,否則不要告訴別人該怎麼做。

chapters.title: The Frogs and the Ox 青蛙與牛

passages.original: CH An Ox came down to a reedy pool to drink. As he splashed heavily into the water, he crushed a young Frog into the mud. The old Frog soon missed the little one and asked his brothers and sisters what had become of him.
passages.vernacular: 一頭牛嚟到長滿蘆葦嘅池塘邊飲水。佢重重地踩進水裡時,把一隻小青蛙踩進咗爛泥。老青蛙好快發現小嘅唔見喇,就問佢嘅兄弟姐妹牠點喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一頭牛來到長滿蘆葦的池塘邊喝水。他重重地踩進水裡時,把一隻小青蛙踩進了爛泥。老青蛙很快發現小的不見了,就問他的兄弟姐妹牠怎麼了。

passages.original: "A great big monster," said one of them, "stepped on little brother with one of his huge feet!"
passages.vernacular: 「一個大大嘅怪物,」其中一個講,「用牠一隻巨大嘅腳踩咗小弟弟!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「一個大大的怪物,」其中一個說,「用牠一隻巨大的腳踩了小弟弟!」

passages.original: "Big, was he!" said the old Frog, puffing herself up. "Was he as big as this?"
passages.vernacular: 「大?牠有多大?」老青蛙講,一邊把自己鼓起嚟。「有咁大嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「大?牠有多大?」老青蛙說,一邊把自己鼓起來。「有這麼大嗎?」

passages.original: "Oh, much bigger!" they cried.
passages.vernacular: 「哦,大得多!」佢哋喊道。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「哦,大得多!」他們喊道。

passages.original: The Frog puffed up still more.
passages.vernacular: 青蛙鼓得更大喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 青蛙鼓得更大了。

passages.original: "He could not have been bigger than this," she said. But the little Frogs all declared that the monster was much, much bigger and the old Frog kept puffing herself out more and more until, all at once, she burst.
passages.vernacular: 「牠唔可能比呢個更大,」佢講。但小青蛙哋都講嗰怪物大得多、大得多,老青蛙就一直把自己鼓得越嚟越大,直到突然間,佢爆開喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「牠不可能比這個更大,」她說。但小青蛙們都說那怪物大得多、大得多,老青蛙就一直把自己鼓得越來越大,直到突然間,她爆開了。

passages.original: Do not attempt the impossible.
passages.vernacular: 唔好嘗試做唔可能嘅事。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不要嘗試做不可能的事。

chapters.title: The Dog, the Cock, and the Fox 狗、公雞與狐狸

passages.original: CH A Dog and a Cock, who were the best of friends, wished very much to see something of the world. So they decided to leave the farmyard and to set out into the world along the road that led to the woods. The two comrades traveled along in the very best of spirits and without meeting any adventure to speak of.
passages.vernacular: 一隻狗同一隻公雞係最要好嘅朋友,佢哋好想出去睇睇世界。於是佢哋決定離開農場,沿住通往樹林嘅路,出發走進世界。兩個夥伴興高采烈地一路前行,冇遇到乜嘢值得一提嘅冒險。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻狗和一隻公雞是最要好的朋友,他們很想出去看看世界。於是他們決定離開農場,沿著通往樹林的路,出發走進世界。兩個夥伴興高采烈地一路前行,沒遇到什麼值得一提的冒險。

passages.original: At nightfall the Cock, looking for a place to roost, as was his custom, spied nearby a hollow tree that he thought would do very nicely for a night's lodging. The Dog could creep inside and the Cock would fly up on one of the branches. So said, so done, and both slept very comfortably.
passages.vernacular: 天黑時,公雞照佢嘅習慣找個地方棲息,佢睇見附近有一棵空心樹,覺得好適合過夜。狗可以爬進裡面,公雞可以飛到樹枝上。講做就做,兩個都瞓得好舒服。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 天黑時,公雞照他的習慣找個地方棲息,他看見附近有一棵空心樹,覺得很適合過夜。狗可以爬進裡面,公雞可以飛到樹枝上。說做就做,兩個都睡得很舒服。

passages.original: With the first glimmer of dawn the Cock awoke. For the moment he forgot just where he was. He thought he was still in the farmyard where it had been his duty to arouse the household at daybreak. So standing on tip-toes he flapped his wings and crowed lustily. But instead of awakening the farmer, he awakened a Fox not far off in the wood. The Fox immediately had rosy visions of a very delicious breakfast. Hurrying to the tree where the Cock was roosting, he said very politely:
passages.vernacular: 黎明第一縷微光出現時,公雞醒喇。一時間佢忘咗自己喺邊度。佢以為自己仲喺農場,喺嗰度佢嘅職責係喺天亮時叫醒一家人。於是佢踮起腳尖,拍拍翅膀,放聲高啼。但佢冇叫醒農夫,卻吵醒咗不遠處樹林裡嘅一隻狐狸。狐狸即刻眼前浮現一頓美味早餐嘅美好景象。佢急忙跑到公雞棲息嘅樹下,好客氣地講:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 黎明第一縷微光出現時,公雞醒了。一時間他忘了自己在哪裡。他以為自己還在農場,在那裡他的職責是在天亮時叫醒一家人。於是他踮起腳尖,拍拍翅膀,放聲高啼。但他沒有叫醒農夫,卻吵醒了不遠處樹林裡的一隻狐狸。狐狸立刻眼前浮現一頓美味早餐的美好景象。他急忙跑到公雞棲息的樹下,非常客氣地說:

passages.original: "A hearty welcome to our woods, honored sir. I cannot tell you how glad I am to see you here. I am quite sure we shall become the closest of friends."
passages.vernacular: 「熱烈歡迎你嚟到我哋嘅樹林,尊貴嘅先生。我講不出見到你喺呢度我有多高興。我敢肯定我哋會成為最親密嘅朋友。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「熱烈歡迎你來到我們的樹林,尊貴的先生。我說不出見到你在這裡我有多高興。我敢肯定我們會成為最親密的朋友。」

passages.original: "I feel highly flattered, kind sir," replied the Cock slyly. "If you will please go around to the door of my house at the foot of the tree, my porter will let you in."
passages.vernacular: 「我感到好榮幸,好心嘅先生,」公雞狡猾地回答。「如果你肯繞到樹腳下我家嘅門口,我嘅門房會讓你進嚟。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我感到非常榮幸,好心的先生,」公雞狡猾地回答。「如果你肯繞到樹腳下我家的門口,我的門房會讓你進來。」

passages.original: The hungry but unsuspecting Fox, went around the tree as he was told, and in a twinkling the Dog had seized him.
passages.vernacular: 飢餓卻毫無戒心嘅狐狸,照佢講嘅繞到樹嘅另一邊,轉眼間狗就把佢抓住喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 飢餓卻毫無戒心的狐狸,照他說的繞到樹的另一邊,轉眼間狗就把他抓住了。

passages.original: Those who try to deceive may expect to be paid in their own coin.
passages.vernacular: 企圖欺騙別人嘅人,可以預料會得到以牙仲牙嘅報應。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 企圖欺騙別人的人,可以預料會得到以牙還牙的報應。

chapters.title: Belling the Cat 給貓繫鈴鐺

passages.original: CH The Mice once called a meeting to decide on a plan to free themselves of their enemy, the Cat. At least they wished to find some way of knowing when she was coming, so they might have time to run away. Indeed, something had to be done, for they lived in such constant fear of her claws that they hardly dared stir from their dens by night or day.
passages.vernacular: 老鼠哋曾經開會,商量一個辦法,擺脫佢哋嘅敵人——貓。至少佢哋想找個辦法,知道佢乜嘢時候嚟,好有時間逃走。確實必須想點辦法,因為佢哋生活喺對佢爪子嘅持續恐懼之中,日夜都幾乎唔敢從洞裡出嚟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 老鼠們曾經開會,商量一個辦法,擺脫他們的敵人——貓。至少他們想找個辦法,知道她什麼時候來,好有時間逃走。確實必須想點辦法,因為他們生活在對她爪子的持續恐懼之中,日夜都幾乎不敢從洞裡出來。

passages.original: Many plans were discussed, but none of them was thought good enough. At last a very young Mouse got up and said:
passages.vernacular: 討論咗好多辦法,但冇一個被認為夠好。最後一隻好年輕嘅老鼠站起來講:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 討論了很多辦法,但沒有一個被認為夠好。最後一隻很年輕的老鼠站起來說:

passages.original: "I have a plan that seems very simple, but I know it will be successful. All we have to do is to hang a bell about the Cat's neck. When we hear the bell ringing we will know immediately that our enemy is coming."
passages.vernacular: 「我有一個辦法,睇起嚟好簡單,但我知道佢一定會成功。我哋要做嘅只係把一個鈴鐺掛喺貓嘅脖子上。聽到鈴聲響,我哋就即刻知道敵人嚟喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我有一個辦法,看起來很簡單,但我知道它一定會成功。我們要做的只是把一個鈴鐺掛在貓的脖子上。聽到鈴聲響,我們就立刻知道敵人來了。」

passages.original: All the Mice were much surprised that they had not thought of such a plan before. But in the midst of the rejoicing over their good fortune, an old Mouse arose and said:
passages.vernacular: 所有老鼠都好驚訝,佢哋以前點冇想到咁樣嘅辦法。不過正當大家為佢哋嘅好運而歡欣時,一隻老鼠站起來講:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 所有老鼠都很驚訝,他們以前怎麼沒有想到這樣的辦法。可是正當大家為他們的好運而歡欣時,一隻老鼠站起來說:

passages.original: "I will say that the plan of the young Mouse is very good. But let me ask one question: Who will bell the Cat?"
passages.vernacular: 「我得講,呢隻年輕老鼠嘅辦法好好。不過讓我問一個問題:邊個去畀貓繫鈴鐺?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我得說,這隻年輕老鼠的辦法很好。不過讓我問一個問題:誰去給貓繫鈴鐺?」

passages.original: It is one thing to say that something should be done, but quite a different matter to do it.
passages.vernacular: 講應該做某件事係一回事,真嘅去做又係完全不同嘅另一回事。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 說應該做某件事是一回事,真的去做又是完全不同的另一回事。

chapters.title: The Eagle and the Jackdaw 老鷹與寒鴉

passages.original: CH An Eagle, swooping down on powerful wings, seized a lamb in her talons and made off with it to her nest. A Jackdaw saw the deed, and his silly head was filled with the idea that he was big and strong enough to do as the Eagle had done. So with much rustling of feathers and a fierce air, he came down swiftly on the back of a large Ram. But when he tried to rise again he found that he could not get away, for his claws were tangled in the wool. And so far was he from carrying away the Ram, that the Ram hardly noticed he was there.
passages.vernacular: 一隻老鷹用強有力嘅翅膀俯衝下嚟,用爪子抓住一隻小羊,帶住牠飛回巢裡去喇。一隻寒鴉睇見咗呢一幕,佢愚蠢嘅腦袋裡充滿咗一個想法:佢又大又強壯,可以做老鷹所做嘅事。於是佢沙沙作響地抖動羽毛,擺出一副兇猛嘅樣子,快速地降落喺一隻大公羊嘅背上。不過當佢想再飛起嚟時,卻發現無法脫身,因為佢嘅爪子纏喺羊毛裡喇。佢唔好講把公羊帶走,公羊幾乎都冇注意到佢喺嗰度。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻老鷹用強有力的翅膀俯衝下來,用爪子抓住一隻小羊,帶著牠飛回巢裡去了。一隻寒鴉看見了這一幕,他愚蠢的腦袋裡充滿了一個想法:他又大又強壯,可以做老鷹所做的事。於是他沙沙作響地抖動羽毛,擺出一副兇猛的樣子,快速地降落在一隻大公羊的背上。可是當他想再飛起來時,卻發現無法脫身,因為他的爪子纏在羊毛裡了。他別說把公羊帶走,公羊幾乎都沒注意到他在那裡。

passages.original: The Shepherd saw the fluttering Jackdaw and at once guessed what had happened. Running up, he caught the bird and clipped its wings. That evening he gave the Jackdaw to his children.
passages.vernacular: 牧羊人睇見拍打住翅膀嘅寒鴉,即刻猜到發生咗乜嘢事。佢跑過去,抓住嗰隻鳥,剪掉咗牠嘅翅膀。嗰天晚上,佢把寒鴉畀咗佢嘅細路哋。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 牧羊人看見拍打著翅膀的寒鴉,馬上猜到發生了什麼事。他跑過去,抓住那隻鳥,剪掉了牠的翅膀。那天晚上,他把寒鴉給了他的孩子們。

passages.original: "What a funny bird this is!" they said laughing, "what do you call it, father?"
passages.vernacular: 「呢個係隻幾咁有趣嘅鳥啊!」佢哋笑住講,「爸爸,呢叫乜嘢?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這是隻多麼有趣的鳥啊!」他們笑著說,「爸爸,這叫什麼?」

passages.original: "That is a Jackdaw, my children. But if you should ask him, he would say he is an Eagle."
passages.vernacular: 「呢個係寒鴉,細路哋。不過如果你去問牠,牠會講牠係老鷹。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這是寒鴉,孩子們。不過如果你去問牠,牠會說牠是老鷹。」

passages.original: Do not let your vanity make you overestimate your powers.
passages.vernacular: 唔好讓你嘅虛榮心使你高估自己嘅能力。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不要讓你的虛榮心使你高估自己的能力。

chapters.title: The Boy and the Filberts 男孩與榛子

passages.original: CH A Boy was given permission to put his hand into a pitcher to get some filberts. But he took such a great fistful that he could not draw his hand out again. There he stood, unwilling to give up a single filbert and yet unable to get them all out at once. Vexed and disappointed he began to cry.
passages.vernacular: 一個男孩得到許可,可以把手伸進一個罐子裡攞啲榛子。不過佢抓咗滿滿一大把,結果手抽不出嚟喇。佢就站喺嗰度,唔願意放棄任何一顆榛子,卻又唔能夠一下子把佢哋都攞出嚟。佢又煩惱又失望,開始哭起嚟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一個男孩得到許可,可以把手伸進一個罐子裡拿一些榛子。可是他抓了滿滿一大把,結果手抽不出來了。他就站在那裡,不願意放棄任何一顆榛子,卻又不能一下子把它們都拿出來。他又煩惱又失望,開始哭起來。

passages.original: "My boy," said his mother, "be satisfied with half the nuts you have taken and you will easily get your hand out. Then perhaps you may have some more filberts some other time."
passages.vernacular: 「細路,」佢母親講,「把你抓嘅榛子放下一半,你就好容易把手攞出嚟喇。或者以後你仲有機會食到更多榛子。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「孩子,」他母親說,「把你抓的榛子放下一半,你就很容易把手拿出來了。也許以後你還有機會吃到更多榛子。」

passages.original: Do not attempt too much at once.
passages.vernacular: 唔好一次嘗試得太多。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不要一次嘗試得太多。

chapters.title: Hercules and the Wagoner 海格力斯與車夫

passages.original: CH A Farmer was driving his wagon along a miry country road after a heavy rain. The horses could hardly drag the load through the deep mud, and at last came to a standstill when one of the wheels sank to the hub in a rut.
passages.vernacular: 一個農夫喺大雨過後,趕住佢嘅馬車走喺一條泥濘嘅鄉村路上。馬匹幾乎拉不動貨物走過深深嘅泥濘,最後停咗下嚟,因為一個車輪陷進車轍,一直沉到輪轂。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一個農夫在大雨過後,趕著他的馬車走在一條泥濘的鄉村路上。馬匹幾乎拉不動貨物走過深深的泥濘,最後停了下來,因為一個車輪陷進車轍,一直沉到輪轂。

passages.original: The farmer climbed down from his seat and stood beside the wagon looking at it but without making the least effort to get it out of the rut. All he did was to curse his bad luck and call loudly on Hercules to come to his aid. Then, it is said, Hercules really did appear, saying:
passages.vernacular: 農夫從座位上爬下嚟,站喺馬車旁邊睇住佢,卻啲都冇努力把佢弄出車轍。佢只係咒罵自己運氣不好,大聲呼喚海格力斯嚟幫助佢。據講,海格力斯真嘅出現喇,講:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 農夫從座位上爬下來,站在馬車旁邊看著它,卻一點也沒有努力把它弄出車轍。他只是咒罵自己運氣不好,大聲呼喚海格力斯來幫助他。據說,海格力斯真的出現了,說:

passages.original: "Put your shoulder to the wheel, man, and urge on your horses. Do you think you can move the wagon by simply looking at it and whining about it? Hercules will not help unless you make some effort to help yourself."
passages.vernacular: 「伙計,把你嘅肩膀頂喺車輪上,催你嘅馬前進。你以為光睇住馬車、對住佢哀歎就能讓佢動起嚟嗎?除非你自己努力幫自己,否則海格力斯係唔會幫你嘅。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「伙計,把你的肩膀頂在車輪上,催你的馬前進。你以為光看著馬車、對著它哀歎就能讓它動起來嗎?除非你自己努力幫自己,否則海格力斯是不會幫你的。」

passages.original: And when the farmer put his shoulder to the wheel and urged on the horses, the wagon moved very readily, and soon the Farmer was riding along in great content and with a good lesson learned.
passages.vernacular: 當農夫把肩膀頂喺車輪上、催馬前進時,馬車好容易就動喇,不久農夫就心滿意足地駕車前行,並且學到咗一個好教訓。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 當農夫把肩膀頂在車輪上、催馬前進時,馬車很容易就動了,不久農夫就心滿意足地駕車前行,並且學到了一個好教訓。

passages.original: Self help is the best help.
passages.vernacular: 自助者天助。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 自助者天助。

passages.original: Heaven helps those who help themselves.
passages.vernacular: 天助自助者。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 天助自助者。

chapters.title: The Kid and the Wolf 小山羊與狼

passages.original: CH A frisky young Kid had been left by the herdsman on the thatched roof of a sheep shelter to keep him out of harm's way. The Kid was browsing near the edge of the roof, when he spied a Wolf and began to jeer at him, making faces and abusing him to his heart's content.
passages.vernacular: 一隻活潑嘅小山羊被牧人留喺羊舍嘅茅草屋頂上,讓佢別出乜嘢危險。小山羊喺屋頂邊緣附近食草時,睇見一隻狼,就開始嘲笑佢,做鬼臉,盡情辱罵佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻活潑的小山羊被牧人留在羊舍的茅草屋頂上,讓他別出什麼危險。小山羊在屋頂邊緣附近吃草時,看見一隻狼,就開始嘲笑他,做鬼臉,盡情辱罵他。

passages.original: "I hear you," said the Wolf, "and I haven't the least grudge against you for what you say or do. When you are up there it is the roof that's talking, not you."
passages.vernacular: 「我聽到你喇,」狼講,「我對你所講所做嘅啲都不記恨。你喺嗰上面嘅時候,係屋頂喺講話,唔係你。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我聽到你了,」狼說,「我對你所說所做的一點也不記恨。你在那上面的時候,是屋頂在說話,不是你。」

passages.original: Do not say anything at any time that you would not say at all times.
passages.vernacular: 唔好喺任何時候講你唔會喺所有時候都講嘅話。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不要在任何時候說你不會在所有時候都說的話。

chapters.title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse 城市老鼠與鄉下老鼠

passages.original: CH A Town Mouse once visited a relative who lived in the country. For lunch the Country Mouse served wheat stalks, roots, and acorns, with a dash of cold water for drink. The Town Mouse ate very sparingly, nibbling a little of this and a little of that, and by her manner making it very plain that she ate the simple food only to be polite.
passages.vernacular: 一隻城裡嘅老鼠有一次去拜訪住喺鄉下嘅親戚。午飯時,鄉下老鼠端上麥稈、草根同橡實,仲有啲兒涼水當飲料。城裡老鼠食得好少,呢兒啃啲,嗰兒啃啲,從佢嘅態度可以好明顯睇出,佢食呢簡單嘅食物只係出於禮貌。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻城裡的老鼠有一次去拜訪住在鄉下的親戚。午飯時,鄉下老鼠端上麥稈、草根和橡實,還有一點兒涼水當飲料。城裡老鼠吃得很少,這兒啃一點,那兒啃一點,從她的態度可以很明顯看出,她吃這簡單的食物只是出於禮貌。

passages.original: After the meal the friends had a long talk, or rather the Town Mouse talked about her life in the city while the Country Mouse listened. They then went to bed in a cozy nest in the hedgerow and slept in quiet and comfort until morning. In her sleep the Country Mouse dreamed she was a Town Mouse with all the luxuries and delights of city life that her friend had described for her. So the next day when the Town Mouse asked the Country Mouse to go home with her to the city, she gladly said yes.
passages.vernacular: 飯後朋友哋談咗好久,或者講係城裡老鼠談佢喺城裡嘅生活,鄉下老鼠聽住。然後佢哋到籬笆下一個舒適嘅窩裡瞓覺,安安靜靜、舒舒服服地瞓到天亮。瞓夢中,鄉下老鼠夢見自己成咗一隻城裡老鼠,享受住朋友為佢描述嘅城市生活嘅一切奢華同樂趣。所以第二天,城裡老鼠請鄉下老鼠同佢一起回城裡時,佢高興地答應喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 飯後朋友們談了很久,或者說是城裡老鼠談她在城裡的生活,鄉下老鼠聽著。然後她們到籬笆下一個舒適的窩裡睡覺,安安靜靜、舒舒服服地睡到天亮。睡夢中,鄉下老鼠夢見自己成了一隻城裡老鼠,享受著朋友為她描述的城市生活的一切奢華和樂趣。所以第二天,城裡老鼠請鄉下老鼠和她一起回城裡時,她高興地答應了。

passages.original: When they reached the mansion in which the Town Mouse lived, they found on the table in the dining room the leavings of a very fine banquet. There were sweetmeats and jellies, pastries, delicious cheeses, indeed, the most tempting foods that a Mouse can imagine. But just as the Country Mouse was about to nibble a dainty bit of pastry, she heard a Cat mew loudly and scratch at the door. In great fear the Mice scurried to a hiding place, where they lay quite still for a long time, hardly daring to breathe. When at last they ventured back to the feast, the door opened suddenly and in came the servants to clear the table, followed by the House Dog.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋到達城裡老鼠住嘅大宅子時,發現餐廳嘅桌上仲留住一頓盛宴嘅殘餘。有蜜餞、果凍、糕點、美味嘅乳酪,確實係一隻老鼠所能想像嘅最誘人嘅食物。不過正當鄉下老鼠要啃一小塊精緻嘅糕點時,佢聽到一隻貓大聲喵喵叫,並喺門上抓撓。老鼠哋嚇得趕緊跑到一個藏身嘅地方,喺嗰度一動不動地躺咗好久,幾乎唔敢呼吸。最後佢哋冒險回到宴席上時,門突然打開喇,僕人哋進嚟收拾桌子,後面跟住家裡嘅狗。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她們到達城裡老鼠住的大宅子時,發現餐廳的桌上還留著一頓盛宴的殘餘。有蜜餞、果凍、糕點、美味的乳酪,確實是一隻老鼠所能想像的最誘人的食物。可是正當鄉下老鼠要啃一小塊精緻的糕點時,她聽到一隻貓大聲喵喵叫,並在門上抓撓。老鼠們嚇得趕緊跑到一個藏身的地方,在那裡一動不動地躺了很久,幾乎不敢呼吸。最後她們冒險回到宴席上時,門突然打開了,僕人們進來收拾桌子,後面跟著家裡的狗。

passages.original: The Country Mouse stopped in the Town Mouse's den only long enough to pick up her carpet bag and umbrella.
passages.vernacular: 鄉下老鼠喺城裡老鼠嘅洞裡只停咗一下,攞咗佢嘅旅行包同雨傘。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 鄉下老鼠在城裡老鼠的洞裡只停了一下,拿了她的旅行包和雨傘。

passages.original: "You may have luxuries and dainties that I have not," she said as she hurried away, "but I prefer my plain food and simple life in the country with the peace and security that go with it."
passages.vernacular: 「你或者有我冇嘅奢侈品同美食,」佢匆匆離去時講,「不過我更鍾意我嘅粗茶淡飯同鄉下簡單嘅生活,以及隨之而嚟嘅平靜同安全。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你也許有我沒有的奢侈品和美食,」她匆匆離去時說,「可是我更喜歡我的粗茶淡飯和鄉下簡單的生活,以及隨之而來的平靜和安全。」

passages.original: Poverty with security is better than plenty in the midst of fear and uncertainty.
passages.vernacular: 有安全感嘅貧窮,勝過喺恐懼同不安中嘅富足。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 有安全感的貧窮,勝過在恐懼和不安中的富足。

chapters.title: The Fox and the Grapes 狐狸與葡萄

passages.original: CH A Fox one day spied a beautiful bunch of ripe grapes hanging from a vine trained along the branches of a tree. The grapes seemed ready to burst with juice, and the Fox's mouth watered as he gazed longingly at them.
passages.vernacular: 有一天,一隻狐狸睇見一串漂亮嘅熟葡萄,掛喺攀附於樹枝上嘅葡萄藤上。葡萄似乎飽滿得快要爆出汁嚟,狐狸盯住佢哋,渴望得直流口水。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 有一天,一隻狐狸看見一串漂亮的熟葡萄,掛在攀附於樹枝上的葡萄藤上。葡萄似乎飽滿得快要爆出汁來,狐狸盯著它們,渴望得直流口水。

passages.original: The bunch hung from a high branch, and the Fox had to jump for it. The first time he jumped he missed it by a long way. So he walked off a short distance and took a running leap at it, only to fall short once more. Again and again he tried, but in vain.
passages.vernacular: 嗰串葡萄掛喺高高嘅樹枝上,狐狸得跳起嚟才夠得住。佢第一次跳起嚟,差得好遠。於是佢走開一小段距離,助跑住撲上去,結果又夠唔到。佢一次又一次地試,卻徒勞無功。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 那串葡萄掛在高高的樹枝上,狐狸得跳起來才夠得著。他第一次跳起來,差得很遠。於是他走開一小段距離,助跑著撲上去,結果又夠不到。他一次又一次地試,卻徒勞無功。

passages.original: Now he sat down and looked at the grapes in disgust.
passages.vernacular: 而家佢坐下嚟,厭惡地睇住葡萄。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 現在他坐下來,厭惡地看著葡萄。

passages.original: "What a fool I am," he said. "Here I am wearing myself out to get a bunch of sour grapes that are not worth gaping for."
passages.vernacular: 「我真係個傻瓜,」佢講。「我喺呢度累得要死,就為了弄到一串不值得張住嘴盼望嘅酸葡萄。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我真是個傻瓜,」他說。「我在這裡累得要死,就為了弄到一串不值得張著嘴盼望的酸葡萄。」

passages.original: And off he walked very, very scornfully.
passages.vernacular: 於是佢好、好不屑地走開喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 於是他非常、非常不屑地走開了。

passages.original: There are many who pretend to despise and belittle that which is beyond their reach.
passages.vernacular: 有許多人假裝輕視同貶低佢哋夠唔到嘅嘢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 有許多人假裝輕視和貶低他們夠不到的東西。

chapters.title: The Bundle of Sticks 一捆樹枝

passages.original: CH A certain Father had a family of Sons, who were forever quarreling among themselves. No words he could say did the least good, so he cast about in his mind for some very striking example that should make them see that discord would lead them to misfortune.
passages.vernacular: 有一位父親,佢嘅幾個兒子總是互相爭吵。佢講乜嘢話都冇啲用處,於是佢喺心裡琢磨,想找一個好醒目的例子,讓佢哋明白不同會把佢哋引向不幸。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 有一位父親,他的幾個兒子總是互相爭吵。他說什麼話都沒有一點用處,於是他在心裡琢磨,想找一個非常醒目的例子,讓他們明白不和會把他們引向不幸。

passages.original: One day when the quarreling had been much more violent than usual and each of the Sons was moping in a surly manner, he asked one of them to bring him a bundle of sticks. Then handing the bundle to each of his Sons in turn he told them to try to break it. But although each one tried his best, none was able to do so.
passages.vernacular: 有一天,爭吵比平常激烈得多,每個兒子都悶悶不樂、一臉陰沉,佢叫其中一個去攞一捆樹枝嚟。然後佢把呢捆樹枝依次遞畀每個兒子,叫佢哋試住折斷佢。不過儘管每個人都盡咗全力,冇一個能折斷。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 有一天,爭吵比平常激烈得多,每個兒子都悶悶不樂、一臉陰沉,他叫其中一個去拿一捆樹枝來。然後他把這捆樹枝依次遞給每個兒子,叫他們試著折斷它。可是儘管每個人都盡了全力,沒有一個能折斷。

passages.original: The Father then untied the bundle and gave the sticks to his Sons to break one by one. This they did very easily.
passages.vernacular: 父親於是解開嗰捆樹枝,把樹枝畀兒子哋,讓佢哋一根一根地折。佢哋好容易就做到喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 父親於是解開那捆樹枝,把樹枝給兒子們,讓他們一根一根地折。他們很容易就做到了。

passages.original: "My Sons," said the Father, "do you not see how certain it is that if you agree with each other and help each other, it will be impossible for your enemies to injure you? But if you are divided among yourselves, you will be no stronger than a single stick in that bundle."
passages.vernacular: 「我嘅細路哋,」父親講,「你哋不明白嗎?如果你哋彼此團結,互相幫助,你哋嘅敵人肯定無法傷害你哋。但如果你哋自己分裂,你哋就不過像嗰捆樹枝裡嘅一根樹枝一樣弱。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我的孩子們,」父親說,「你們不明白嗎?如果你們彼此團結,互相幫助,你們的敵人肯定無法傷害你們。但如果你們自己分裂,你們就不過像那捆樹枝裡的一根樹枝一樣弱。」

passages.original: In unity is strength.
passages.vernacular: 團結就係力量。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 團結就是力量。

chapters.title: The Wolf and the Crane 狼與鶴

passages.original: CH A Wolf had been feasting too greedily, and a bone had stuck crosswise in his throat. He could get it neither up nor down, and of course he could not eat a thing. Naturally that was an awful state of affairs for a greedy Wolf.
passages.vernacular: 一隻狼食得太貪婪,一塊骨頭橫住卡喺佢嘅喉嚨裡。佢不上不下,當然乜嘢都食不喇。對一隻貪食嘅狼來講,呢自然係糟透咗嘅境況。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻狼吃得太貪婪,一塊骨頭橫著卡在他的喉嚨裡。他不上不下,當然什麼也吃不了。對一隻貪吃的狼來說,這自然是糟透了的境況。

passages.original: So away he hurried to the Crane. He was sure that she, with her long neck and bill, would easily be able to reach the bone and pull it out.
passages.vernacular: 於是佢匆忙跑去找鶴。佢確信佢憑住長脖子同長嘴,一定好容易夠到骨頭並把佢拔出嚟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 於是他匆忙跑去找鶴。他確信她憑著長脖子和長嘴,一定很容易夠到骨頭並把它拔出來。

passages.original: "I will reward you very handsomely," said the Wolf, "if you pull that bone out for me."
passages.vernacular: 「如果你替我把嗰塊骨頭拔出嚟,」狼講,「我會重重地酬謝你。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「如果你替我把那塊骨頭拔出來,」狼說,「我會重重地酬謝你。」

passages.original: The Crane, as you can imagine, was very uneasy about putting her head in a Wolf's throat. But she was grasping in nature, so she did what the Wolf asked her to do.
passages.vernacular: 你可以想像,鶴把頭伸進狼嘅喉嚨裡,好不安。但佢本性貪心,所以定係照狼講嘅做喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 你可以想像,鶴把頭伸進狼的喉嚨裡,非常不安。但她本性貪心,所以還是照狼說的做了。

passages.original: When the Wolf felt that the bone was gone, he started to walk away.
passages.vernacular: 狼覺得骨頭冇喇,就邁步要走。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 狼覺得骨頭沒有了,就邁步要走。

passages.original: "But what about my reward!" called the Crane anxiously.
passages.vernacular: 「不過我嘅酬謝呢!」鶴焦急地喊道。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「可是我的酬謝呢!」鶴焦急地喊道。

passages.original: "What!" snarled the Wolf, whirling around. "Haven't you got it? Isn't it enough that I let you take your head out of my mouth without snapping it off?"
passages.vernacular: 「乜嘢!」狼轉過身,咆哮道。「你仲冇攞到嗎?我讓你把頭從我嘴裡抽出去而冇把佢咬斷,難道仲唔夠嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「什麼!」狼轉過身,咆哮道。「你還沒拿到嗎?我讓你把頭從我嘴裡抽出去而沒把它咬斷,難道還不夠嗎?」

passages.original: Expect no reward for serving the wicked.
passages.vernacular: 為惡人效勞,別指望報酬。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 為惡人效勞,別指望報酬。

chapters.title: The Ass and His Driver 驢子與趕驢人

passages.original: CH An Ass was being driven along a road leading down the mountain side, when he suddenly took it into his silly head to choose his own path. He could see his stall at the foot of the mountain, and to him the quickest way down seemed to be over the edge of the nearest cliff. Just as he was about to leap over, his master caught him by the tail and tried to pull him back, but the stubborn Ass would not yield and pulled with all his might.
passages.vernacular: 一頭驢子正被人趕住走喺一條下山嘅路上,佢突然異想天開,要自己選一條路。佢能睇見山腳下嘅馬廄,喺佢睇來,最快嘅下山辦法似乎係從最近嘅懸崖邊上跳下去。就喺佢要跳下去時,主人抓住咗佢嘅尾巴,想把佢拉回嚟,但倔強嘅驢子唔肯讓步,使出渾身力氣往前拉。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一頭驢子正被人趕著走在一條下山的路上,他突然異想天開,要自己選一條路。他能看見山腳下的馬廄,在他看來,最快的下山辦法似乎是從最近的懸崖邊上跳下去。就在他要跳下去時,主人抓住了他的尾巴,想把他拉回來,但倔強的驢子不肯讓步,使出渾身力氣往前拉。

passages.original: "Very well," said his master, "go your way, you willful beast, and see where it leads you."
passages.vernacular: 「好吧,」佢主人講,「你呢任性嘅畜生,走你嘅路吧,睇睇佢把你帶到邊度去。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「好吧,」他主人說,「你這任性的畜生,走你的路吧,看看它把你帶到哪裡去。」

passages.original: With that he let go, and the foolish Ass tumbled head over heels down the mountain side.
passages.vernacular: 講完佢鬆咗手,愚蠢嘅驢子就翻住跟頭滾下山坡。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 說完他鬆了手,愚蠢的驢子就翻著跟頭滾下山坡。

passages.original: They who will not listen to reason but stubbornly go their own way against the friendly advice of those who are wiser than they, are on the road to misfortune.
passages.vernacular: 嗰啲唔肯聽從道理、固執地違背比自己更聰明嘅人嘅友好勸告而一意孤行嘅人,正走喺通向不幸嘅路上。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 那些不肯聽從道理、固執地違背比自己更聰明的人的友好勸告而一意孤行的人,正走在通向不幸的路上。

chapters.title: The Oxen and the Wheels 牛與車輪

passages.original: CH A pair of Oxen were drawing a heavily loaded wagon along a miry country road. They had to use all their strength to pull the wagon, but they did not complain.
passages.vernacular: 一對牛正拉住一輛重載嘅馬車走喺泥濘嘅鄉村路上。佢哋必須使出全部力氣嚟拉馬車,但並不抱怨。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一對牛正拉著一輛重載的馬車走在泥濘的鄉村路上。他們必須使出全部力氣來拉馬車,但並不抱怨。

passages.original: The Wheels of the wagon were of a different sort. Though the task they had to do was very light compared with that of the Oxen, they creaked and groaned at every turn. The poor Oxen, pulling with all their might to draw the wagon through the deep mud, had their ears filled with the loud complaining of the Wheels. And this, you may well know, made their work so much the harder to endure.
passages.vernacular: 馬車嘅車輪卻係另一種樣子。雖然同牛嘅活兒相比,佢哋要做嘅工作好輕,但佢哋每轉一圈都吱嘎呻吟。可憐嘅牛使盡全力拉住車穿過深深嘅泥濘,耳朵裡卻灌滿咗車輪嘅大聲抱怨。而你好清楚,呢使佢哋嘅工作更加難以忍受。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 馬車的車輪卻是另一種樣子。雖然與牛的活兒相比,它們要做的工作很輕,但它們每轉一圈都吱嘎呻吟。可憐的牛使盡全力拉著車穿過深深的泥濘,耳朵裡卻灌滿了車輪的大聲抱怨。而你很清楚,這使他們的工作更加難以忍受。

passages.original: "Silence!" the Oxen cried at last, out of patience. "What have you Wheels to complain about so loudly? We are drawing all the weight, not you, and we are keeping still about it besides."
passages.vernacular: 「閉嘴!」牛終於忍無可忍地喊道。「你哋呢啲車輪有乜嘢好咁大聲抱怨嘅?係我哋喺拉全部重量,唔係你哋,而且我哋仲一聲不吭呢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「閉嘴!」牛終於忍無可忍地喊道。「你們這些車輪有什麼好這麼大聲抱怨的?是我們在拉全部重量,不是你們,而且我們還一聲不吭呢。」

passages.original: They complain most who suffer least.
passages.vernacular: 受苦最少嘅人,抱怨得最多。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 受苦最少的人,抱怨得最多。

chapters.title: The Lion and the Mouse 獅子與老鼠

passages.original: CH A Lion lay asleep in the forest, his great head resting on his paws. A timid little Mouse came upon him unexpectedly, and in her fright and haste to get away, ran across the Lion's nose. Roused from his nap, the Lion laid his huge paw angrily on the tiny creature to kill her.
passages.vernacular: 一隻獅子躺喺森林裡瞓覺,佢嘅大腦袋枕喺爪子上。一隻膽小嘅小老鼠意外地碰上咗佢,驚慌失措、急住逃走時,從獅子嘅鼻子上跑咗過去。獅子從瞓夢中被驚醒,生氣地把佢巨大嘅爪子按喺嗰小生物身上,要殺死佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻獅子躺在森林裡睡覺,他的大腦袋枕在爪子上。一隻膽小的小老鼠意外地碰上了他,驚慌失措、急著逃走時,從獅子的鼻子上跑了過去。獅子從睡夢中被驚醒,生氣地把他巨大的爪子按在那小生物身上,要殺死她。

passages.original: "Spare me!" begged the poor Mouse. "Please let me go and some day I will surely repay you."
passages.vernacular: 「饒咗我吧!」可憐嘅老鼠哀求道。「請讓我走,有一天我一定會報答你。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「饒了我吧!」可憐的老鼠哀求道。「請讓我走,有一天我一定會報答你。」

passages.original: The Lion was much amused to think that a Mouse could ever help him. But he was generous and finally let the Mouse go.
passages.vernacular: 獅子覺得一隻老鼠竟然能幫佢,好好笑。但佢好慷慨,最後讓老鼠走喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 獅子覺得一隻老鼠竟然能幫他,非常好笑。但他很慷慨,最後讓老鼠走了。

passages.original: Some days later, while stalking his prey in the forest, the Lion was caught in the toils of a hunter's net. Unable to free himself, he filled the forest with his angry roaring. The Mouse knew the voice and quickly found the Lion struggling in the net. Running to one of the great ropes that bound him, she gnawed it until it parted, and soon the Lion was free.
passages.vernacular: 幾天後,獅子喺森林裡追蹤獵物時,被獵人嘅網困住喇。佢無法掙脫,憤怒嘅吼聲響徹森林。老鼠認得嗰個聲音,好快找到咗喺網裡掙扎嘅獅子。佢跑到捆住佢嘅一根大繩子嗰度,咬啊咬,直到佢斷開,不久獅子就自由喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 幾天後,獅子在森林裡追蹤獵物時,被獵人的網困住了。他無法掙脫,憤怒的吼聲響徹森林。老鼠認得那個聲音,很快找到了在網裡掙扎的獅子。她跑到捆著他的一根大繩子那裡,咬啊咬,直到它斷開,不久獅子就自由了。

passages.original: "You laughed when I said I would repay you," said the Mouse. "Now you see that even a Mouse can help a Lion."
passages.vernacular: 「我講我要報答你嘅時候,你笑喇,」老鼠講。「而家你睇見喇,連一隻老鼠都能幫助獅子。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我說我要報答你的時候,你笑了,」老鼠說。「現在你看見了,連一隻老鼠也能幫助獅子。」

passages.original: A kindness is never wasted.
passages.vernacular: 善意永遠唔會白費。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 善意永遠不會白費。

chapters.title: The Shepherd Boy and the Wolf 牧羊男孩與狼

passages.original: CH A Shepherd Boy tended his master's Sheep near a dark forest not far from the village. Soon he found life in the pasture very dull. All he could do to amuse himself was to talk to his dog or play on his shepherd's pipe.
passages.vernacular: 一個牧羊男孩喺離村子不遠嘅一片黑森林旁,照睇佢主人嘅羊。不久佢就覺得牧場上嘅生活好無聊。佢能做嚟消遣嘅,只係同佢嘅狗講話或吹佢嘅牧笛。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一個牧羊男孩在離村子不遠的一片黑森林旁,照看他主人的羊。不久他就覺得牧場上的生活非常無聊。他能做來消遣的,只是同他的狗說話或吹他的牧笛。

passages.original: One day as he sat watching the Sheep and the quiet forest, and thinking what he would do should he see a Wolf, he thought of a plan to amuse himself.
passages.vernacular: 有一天,佢坐住睇住羊群同寧靜嘅森林,想住如果睇見狼自己會點做,佢想出咗一個消遣自己嘅計劃。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 有一天,他坐著看著羊群和寧靜的森林,想著如果看見狼自己會怎麼做,他想出了一個消遣自己的計劃。

passages.original: His Master had told him to call for help should a Wolf attack the flock, and the Villagers would drive it away. So now, though he had not seen anything that even looked like a Wolf, he ran toward the village shouting at the top of his voice, "Wolf! Wolf!"
passages.vernacular: 佢嘅主人曾告訴佢,如果狼襲擊羊群,佢就呼救,村民哋會把狼趕走。所以而家,雖然佢連啲像狼嘅嘢都冇睇見,佢定係朝村子跑去,扯住嗓子大喊:「狼嚟喇!狼嚟喇!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他的主人曾告訴他,如果狼襲擊羊群,他就呼救,村民們會把狼趕走。所以現在,雖然他連一點像狼的東西都沒看見,他還是朝村子跑去,扯著嗓子大喊:「狼來了!狼來了!」

passages.original: As he expected, the Villagers who heard the cry dropped their work and ran in great excitement to the pasture. But when they got there they found the Boy doubled up with laughter at the trick he had played on them.
passages.vernacular: 正如佢預料嘅,聽到喊聲嘅村民放下手頭嘅活,好激動地跑到牧場。不過佢哋到咗嗰度,卻發現男孩對自己耍嘅把戲笑得直不起腰。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 正如他預料的,聽到喊聲的村民放下手頭的活,非常激動地跑到牧場。可是他們到了那裡,卻發現男孩對自己耍的把戲笑得直不起腰。

passages.original: A few days later the Shepherd Boy again shouted, "Wolf! Wolf!" Again the Villagers ran to help him, only to be laughed at again.
passages.vernacular: 幾天後,牧羊男孩又喊:「狼嚟喇!狼嚟喇!」村民哋又跑嚟幫佢,結果又被取笑喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 幾天後,牧羊男孩又喊:「狼來了!狼來了!」村民們又跑來幫他,結果又被取笑了。

passages.original: Then one evening as the sun was setting behind the forest and the shadows were creeping out over the pasture, a Wolf really did spring from the underbrush and fall upon the Sheep.
passages.vernacular: 然後有一天傍晚,太陽落到森林後面,影子爬過牧場,一隻狼真嘅從灌木叢中躍出嚟,撲向羊群。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後有一天傍晚,太陽落到森林後面,影子爬過牧場,一隻狼真的從灌木叢中躍出來,撲向羊群。

passages.original: In terror the Boy ran toward the village shouting "Wolf! Wolf!" But though the Villagers heard the cry, they did not run to help him as they had before. "He cannot fool us again," they said.
passages.vernacular: 男孩驚恐地朝村子跑去,喊住:「狼嚟喇!狼嚟喇!」但係村民哋雖然聽到咗喊聲,卻冇像以前嗰樣跑去幫佢。「佢唔能夠再騙我哋喇,」佢哋講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 男孩驚恐地朝村子跑去,喊著:「狼來了!狼來了!」但是村民們雖然聽到了喊聲,卻沒有像以前那樣跑去幫他。「他不能再騙我們了,」他們說。

passages.original: The Wolf killed a great many of the Boy's sheep and then slipped away into the forest.
passages.vernacular: 狼咬死咗男孩嘅許多羊,然後溜進咗森林。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 狼咬死了男孩的許多羊,然後溜進了森林。

passages.original: Liars are not believed even when they speak the truth.
passages.vernacular: 講謊嘅人,即使講真話,都冇人相信。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 說謊的人,即使說真話,也沒有人相信。

chapters.title: The Gnat and the Bull 蚊蟲與公牛

passages.original: CH A Gnat flew over the meadow with much buzzing for so small a creature and settled on the tip of one of the horns of a Bull. After he had rested a short time, he made ready to fly away. But before he left he begged the Bull's pardon for having used his horn for a resting place.
passages.vernacular: 一隻小蚊蟲飛過草地,對咁小嘅生物來講,嗡嗡聲響好大,佢落喺一頭公牛嘅一隻角尖上。休息咗一小會兒後,佢準備飛走。但喺離開之前,佢向公牛道歉,講自己把牛角當成咗休息嘅地方。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻小蚊蟲飛過草地,對這麼小的生物來說,嗡嗡聲響很大,他落在一頭公牛的一隻角尖上。休息了一小會兒後,他準備飛走。但在離開之前,他向公牛道歉,說自己把牛角當成了休息的地方。

passages.original: "You must be very glad to have me go now," he said.
passages.vernacular: 「你而家一定好高興我走喇,」佢講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你現在一定很高興我走了,」他說。

passages.original: "It's all the same to me," replied the Bull. "I did not even know you were there."
passages.vernacular: 「對我都一樣,」公牛回答。「我甚至唔知道你喺嗰度。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「對我都一樣,」公牛回答。「我甚至不知道你在那裡。」

passages.original: We are often of greater importance in our own eyes than in the eyes of our neighbor.
passages.vernacular: 喺我哋自己眼裡,我哋往往比喺鄰居眼裡重要得多。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 在我們自己眼裡,我們往往比在鄰居眼裡重要得多。

passages.original: The smaller the mind the greater the conceit.
passages.vernacular: 心胸越小,自負越大。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 心胸越小,自負越大。

chapters.title: The Plane Tree 梧桐樹

passages.original: CH Two Travellers, walking in the noonday sun, sought the shade of a widespreading tree to rest. As they lay looking up among the pleasant leaves, they saw that it was a Plane Tree.
passages.vernacular: 兩個旅人喺正午嘅陽光下行走,想喺一棵枝葉茂密嘅大樹嘅蔭涼下歇息。佢哋躺住仰望愜意嘅樹葉時,睇出嗰個係一棵梧桐樹。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 兩個旅人在正午的陽光下行走,想在一棵枝葉茂密的大樹的蔭涼下歇息。他們躺著仰望愜意的樹葉時,看出那是一棵梧桐樹。

passages.original: "How useless is the Plane!" said one of them. "It bears no fruit whatever, and only serves to litter the ground with leaves."
passages.vernacular: 「梧桐樹真冇用!」其中一個講。「佢根本不結果子,只會把地上弄得滿係落葉。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「梧桐樹真沒用!」其中一個說。「它根本不結果子,只會把地上弄得滿是落葉。」

passages.original: "Ungrateful creatures!" said a voice from the Plane Tree. "You lie here in my cooling shade, and yet you say I am useless! Thus ungratefully, O Jupiter, do men receive their blessings!"
passages.vernacular: 「忘恩負義嘅傢伙!」梧桐樹裡傳出一個聲音。「你哋躺喺我涼爽嘅樹蔭下,卻講我冇用!朱比特啊,人類就係咁樣忘恩負義地接受佢哋嘅福氣!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「忘恩負義的傢伙!」梧桐樹裡傳出一個聲音。「你們躺在我涼爽的樹蔭下,卻說我沒用!朱比特啊,人類就是這樣忘恩負義地接受他們的福氣!」

passages.original: Our best blessings are often the least appreciated.
passages.vernacular: 我哋最好嘅福氣,往往係最不被感激嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們最好的福氣,往往是最不被感激的。

chapters.title: The Farmer and the Stork 農夫與鸛

passages.original: CH A Stork of a very simple and trusting nature had been asked by a gay party of Cranes to visit a field that had been newly planted. But the party ended dismally with all the birds entangled in the meshes of the Farmer's net.
passages.vernacular: 一隻性情好單純、容易相信別人嘅鸛,被一群快活嘅鶴邀請,去參觀一塊新播咗種嘅田地。但呢場聚會以悲慘收場,所有嘅鳥都纏喺農夫嘅網眼裡。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻性情非常單純、容易相信別人的鸛,被一群快活的鶴邀請,去參觀一塊新播了種的田地。但這場聚會以悲慘收場,所有的鳥都纏在農夫的網眼裡。

passages.original: The Stork begged the Farmer to spare him.
passages.vernacular: 鸛懇求農夫放過佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 鸛懇求農夫放過他。

passages.original: "Please let me go," he pleaded. "I belong to the Stork family who you know are honest and birds of good character. Besides, I did not know the Cranes were going to steal."
passages.vernacular: 「請讓我走吧,」佢央求道。「我屬於鸛呢個家族,你知道我哋係誠實嘅、品格好嘅鳥。再講,我唔知道嗰啲鶴要去偷嘢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「請讓我走吧,」他央求道。「我屬於鸛這個家族,你知道我們是誠實的、品格好的鳥。再說,我不知道那些鶴要去偷東西。」

passages.original: "You may be a very good bird," answered the Farmer, "but I caught you with the thieving Cranes and you will have to share the same punishment with them."
passages.vernacular: 「你或者係隻好好嘅鳥,」農夫回答,「但我係喺偷嘢嘅鶴群裡抓到你嘅,你得同佢哋受同樣嘅懲罰。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你也許是隻很好的鳥,」農夫回答,「但我是在偷東西的鶴群裡抓到你的,你得和他們受同樣的懲罰。」

passages.original: You are judged by the company you keep.
passages.vernacular: 人家按你交嘅朋友嚟判斷你。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 人家按你交的朋友來判斷你。

chapters.title: The Sheep and the Pig 羊與豬

passages.original: CH One day a shepherd discovered a fat Pig in the meadow where his Sheep were pastured. He very quickly captured the porker, which squealed at the top of its voice the moment the Shepherd laid his hands on it. You would have thought, to hear the loud squealing, that the Pig was being cruelly hurt. But in spite of its squeals and struggles to escape, the Shepherd tucked his prize under his arm and started off to the butcher's in the market place.
passages.vernacular: 有一天,一個牧羊人喺佢嘅羊食草嘅草地上發現咗一隻肥豬。佢好快抓住咗呢頭豬,牧羊人嘅手一碰到牠,牠就扯開嗓子尖叫。聽到嗰響亮嘅尖叫,你會以為呢頭豬正被殘忍地傷害。但儘管牠尖叫掙扎著想逃,牧羊人定係把佢嘅戰利品夾喺腋下,動身往市場上嘅肉店走去。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 有一天,一個牧羊人在他的羊吃草的草地上發現了一隻肥豬。他很快抓住了這頭豬,牧羊人的手一碰到牠,牠就扯開嗓子尖叫。聽到那響亮的尖叫,你會以為這頭豬正被殘忍地傷害。但儘管牠尖叫掙扎著想逃,牧羊人還是把他的戰利品夾在腋下,動身往市場上的肉店走去。

passages.original: The Sheep in the pasture were much astonished and amused at the Pig's behavior, and followed the Shepherd and his charge to the pasture gate.
passages.vernacular: 牧場上嘅羊對豬嘅行為大為驚訝同好笑,跟住牧羊人同佢嘅俘虜走到牧場門口。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 牧場上的羊對豬的行為大為驚訝和好笑,跟著牧羊人和他的俘虜走到牧場門口。

passages.original: "What makes you squeal like that?" asked one of the Sheep. "The Shepherd often catches and carries off one of us. But we should feel very much ashamed to make such a terrible fuss about it like you do."
passages.vernacular: 「你點解嗰樣尖叫?」一隻羊問。「牧羊人常常抓走我哋中嘅一隻。不過我哋會覺得像你咁樣大吵大鬧,係好丟臉嘅事。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你為什麼那樣尖叫?」一隻羊問。「牧羊人常常抓走我們中的一隻。可是我們會覺得像你這樣大吵大鬧,是很丟臉的事。」

passages.original: "That is all very well," replied the Pig, with a squeal and a frantic kick. "When he catches you he is only after your wool. But he wants my bacon! gree-ee-ee!"
passages.vernacular: 「你講得倒好,」豬回答,尖叫一聲,瘋狂地蹬咗一腳。「佢抓你哋,只係要你哋嘅毛。不過佢要嘅係我嘅肉!嗚——嗚——嗚!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你說得倒好,」豬回答,尖叫一聲,瘋狂地蹬了一腳。「他抓你們,只是要你們的毛。可是他要的是我的肉!嗚——嗚——嗚!」

passages.original: It is easy to be brave when there is no danger.
passages.vernacular: 冇危險嘅時候,勇敢係好容易嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 沒有危險的時候,勇敢是很容易的。

chapters.title: The Travelers and the Purse 旅人與錢包

passages.original: CH Two men were traveling in company along the road when one of them picked up a well-filled purse.
passages.vernacular: 兩個人結伴走喺路上,其中一個撿到咗一個鼓鼓嘅錢包。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 兩個人結伴走在路上,其中一個撿到了一個鼓鼓的錢包。

passages.original: "How lucky I am!" he said. "I have found a purse. Judging by its weight it must be full of gold."
passages.vernacular: 「我多幸運啊!」佢講。「我撿到咗一個錢包。從重量睇,裡面一定裝滿咗金子。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我多幸運啊!」他說。「我撿到了一個錢包。從重量看,裡面一定裝滿了金子。」

passages.original: "Do not say 'I have found a purse,'" said his companion. "Say rather 'we have found a purse' and 'how lucky we are.' Travelers ought to share alike the fortunes or misfortunes of the road."
passages.vernacular: 「唔好講『我撿到咗一個錢包』,」佢嘅同伴講。「應該講『我哋撿到咗一個錢包』同『我哋多幸運』。旅行者應該平等地分享路上嘅幸運或不幸。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「不要說『我撿到了一個錢包』,」他的同伴說。「應該說『我們撿到了一個錢包』和『我們多幸運』。旅行者應該平等地分享路上的幸運或不幸。」

passages.original: "No, no," replied the other angrily. "I found it and I am going to keep it."
passages.vernacular: 「不,不,」另一個生氣地回答。「係我撿到嘅,我要留住佢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「不,不,」另一個生氣地回答。「是我撿到的,我要留著它。」

passages.original: Just then they heard a shout of "Stop, thief!" and looking around, saw a mob of people armed with clubs coming down the road.
passages.vernacular: 就喺呢陣,佢哋聽見一聲「站住,小偷!」嘅喊叫,回頭一睇,見到一群手持棍棒嘅人沿住路跑嚟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 就在這時,他們聽見一聲「站住,小偷!」的喊叫,回頭一看,見到一群手持棍棒的人沿著路跑來。

passages.original: The man who had found the purse fell into a panic.
passages.vernacular: 撿到錢包嘅人驚慌失措。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 撿到錢包的人驚慌失措。

passages.original: "We are lost if they find the purse on us," he cried.
passages.vernacular: 「如果佢哋喺我哋身上發現呢個錢包,我哋就完喇,」佢喊道。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「如果他們在我們身上發現這個錢包,我們就完了,」他喊道。

passages.original: "No, no," replied the other, "You would not say 'we' before, so now stick to your 'I'. Say 'I am lost.'"
passages.vernacular: 「不,不,」另一個回答,「你頭先唔肯講『我哋』,而家就堅持你嘅『我』吧。講『我完喇』。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「不,不,」另一個回答,「你剛才不肯說『我們』,現在就堅持你的『我』吧。說『我完了』。」

passages.original: We cannot expect any one to share our misfortunes unless we are willing to share our good fortune also.
passages.vernacular: 除非我哋都願意分享我哋嘅好運,否則我哋唔能夠指望有人分擔我哋嘅不幸。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 除非我們也願意分享我們的好運,否則我們不能指望有人分擔我們的不幸。

chapters.title: The Lion and the Ass 獅子與驢子

passages.original: CH One day as the Lion walked proudly down a forest aisle, and the animals respectfully made way for him, an Ass brayed a scornful remark as he passed.
passages.vernacular: 有一天,獅子驕傲地走喺林間小徑上,動物哋恭敬地畀佢讓路,一頭驢子喺佢經過時,發出一句輕蔑嘅嘶叫。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 有一天,獅子驕傲地走在林間小徑上,動物們恭敬地給他讓路,一頭驢子在他經過時,發出一句輕蔑的嘶叫。

passages.original: The Lion felt a flash of anger. But when he turned his head and saw who had spoken, he walked quietly on. He would not honor the fool with even so much as a stroke of his claws.
passages.vernacular: 獅子心頭閃過一陣怒火。但當佢回過頭,睇到係邊個講嘅,就默默地走開喇。佢不屑於用佢嘅爪子碰呢個傻瓜一下嚟畀佢榮耀。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 獅子心頭閃過一陣怒火。但當他回過頭,看到是誰說的,就默默地走開了。他不屑於用他的爪子碰這個傻瓜一下來給他榮耀。

passages.original: Do not resent the remarks of a fool. Ignore them.
passages.vernacular: 唔好對傻瓜嘅話耿耿於懷。別理佢哋。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不要對傻瓜的話耿耿於懷。別理他們。

chapters.title: The Frogs Who Wished for a King 想要國王的青蛙

passages.original: CH The Frogs were tired of governing themselves. They had so much freedom that it had spoiled them, and they did nothing but sit around croaking in a bored manner and wishing for a government that could entertain them with the pomp and display of royalty, and rule them in a way to make them know they were being ruled. No milk and water government for them, they declared. So they sent a petition to Jupiter asking for a king.
passages.vernacular: 青蛙哋厭倦咗自己管理自己。佢哋嘅自由太多,已經被寵壞喇,佢哋乜嘢都不做,只係坐喺嗰度無聊地呱呱叫,盼望有一個政府,能用王室嘅排場同顯赫嚟娛樂佢哋,並且用一種讓佢哋知道自己被統治嘅方式嚟統治佢哋。佢哋宣稱,唔好乜嘢溫吞水一樣嘅政府。於是佢哋向朱比特遞咗一份請願書,要求一個國王。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 青蛙們厭倦了自己管理自己。他們的自由太多,已經被寵壞了,他們什麼也不做,只是坐在那裡無聊地呱呱叫,盼望有一個政府,能用王室的排場和顯赫來娛樂他們,並且用一種讓他們知道自己被統治的方式來統治他們。他們宣稱,不要什麼溫吞水一樣的政府。於是他們向朱比特遞了一份請願書,要求一個國王。

passages.original: Jupiter saw what simple and foolish creatures they were, but to keep them quiet and make them think they had a king he threw down a huge log, which fell into the water with a great splash. The Frogs hid themselves among the reeds and grasses, thinking the new king to be some fearful giant. But they soon discovered how tame and peaceable King Log was. In a short time the younger Frogs were using him for a diving platform, while the older Frogs made him a meeting place, where they complained loudly to Jupiter about the government.
passages.vernacular: 朱比特睇出佢哋係幾咁單純愚蠢嘅生物,但為了讓佢哋安靜下嚟,並讓佢哋以為有咗國王,佢扔下一根巨大嘅木頭,佢嘩啦一聲掉進水裡。青蛙哋躲進蘆葦同草叢裡,以為新國王係乜嘢可怕嘅巨人。但佢哋好快發現木頭國王係幾咁溫順、平和。不久,年輕嘅青蛙把佢當作跳水台,年老嘅青蛙把佢當作聚會嘅地方,喺嗰度大聲向朱比特抱怨政府。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 朱比特看出他們是多麼單純愚蠢的生物,但為了讓他們安靜下來,並讓他們以為有了國王,他扔下一根巨大的木頭,它嘩啦一聲掉進水裡。青蛙們躲進蘆葦和草叢裡,以為新國王是什麼可怕的巨人。但他們很快發現木頭國王是多麼溫順、平和。不久,年輕的青蛙把他當作跳水台,年老的青蛙把他當作聚會的地方,在那裡大聲向朱比特抱怨政府。

passages.original: To teach the Frogs a lesson the ruler of the gods now sent a Crane to be king of Frogland. The Crane proved to be a very different sort of king from old King Log. He gobbled up the poor Frogs right and left and they soon saw what fools they had been. In mournful croaks they begged Jupiter to take away the cruel tyrant before they should all be destroyed.
passages.vernacular: 為了畀青蛙哋一個教訓,眾神嘅統治者呢次派咗一隻鶴去做青蛙國嘅國王。呢隻鶴證明係同老木頭國王大不相同嘅一種國王。佢左一個右一個地把可憐嘅青蛙哋吞掉,佢哋好快明白自己係幾咁愚蠢。佢哋用哀傷嘅呱呱聲央求朱比特,喺佢哋都被消滅之前,把呢個殘忍嘅暴君帶走。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 為了給青蛙們一個教訓,眾神的統治者這次派了一隻鶴去做青蛙國的國王。這隻鶴證明是與老木頭國王大不相同的一種國王。他左一個右一個地把可憐的青蛙們吞掉,他們很快明白自己是多麼愚蠢。他們用哀傷的呱呱聲央求朱比特,在他們都被消滅之前,把這個殘忍的暴君帶走。

passages.original: "How now!" cried Jupiter "Are you not yet content? You have what you asked for and so you have only yourselves to blame for your misfortunes."
passages.vernacular: 「點回事!」朱比特喊道。「你哋仲不滿足嗎?你哋得到咗你哋所要求嘅,所以你哋嘅不幸只能怪你哋自己。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「怎麼回事!」朱比特喊道。「你們還不滿足嗎?你們得到了你們所要求的,所以你們的不幸只能怪你們自己。」

passages.original: Be sure you can better your condition before you seek to change.
passages.vernacular: 喺尋求改變之前,要確定你能使自己嘅處境變得更好。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 在尋求改變之前,要確定你能使自己的處境變得更好。

chapters.title: The Owl and the Grasshopper 貓頭鷹與蚱蜢

passages.original: CH The Owl always takes her sleep during the day. Then after sundown, when the rosy light fades from the sky and the shadows rise slowly through the wood, out she comes ruffling and blinking from the old hollow tree. Now her weird "hoo-hoo-hoo-oo-oo" echoes through the quiet wood, and she begins her hunt for the bugs and beetles, frogs and mice she likes so well to eat.
passages.vernacular: 貓頭鷹總是喺白天瞓覺。然後日落後,玫瑰色嘅光從天空褪去,影子慢慢升起穿過樹林,佢就搖晃住羽毛、眨住眼睛從老樹洞裡出嚟。而家佢怪異嘅「呼——呼——呼——嗚——嗚」聲喺寂靜嘅樹林裡迴響,佢開始捕捉佢咁愛食嘅蟲子、甲蟲、青蛙同老鼠。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 貓頭鷹總是在白天睡覺。然後日落後,玫瑰色的光從天空褪去,影子慢慢升起穿過樹林,她就搖晃著羽毛、眨著眼睛從老樹洞裡出來。現在她怪異的「呼——呼——呼——嗚——嗚」聲在寂靜的樹林裡迴響,她開始捕捉她那麼愛吃的蟲子、甲蟲、青蛙和老鼠。

passages.original: Now there was a certain old Owl who had become very cross and hard to please as she grew older, especially if anything disturbed her daily slumbers. One warm summer afternoon as she dozed away in her den in the old oak tree, a Grasshopper nearby began a joyous but very raspy song. Out popped the old Owl's head from the opening in the tree that served her both for door and for window.
passages.vernacular: 有一隻老貓頭鷹,隨住年紀漸大,變得好暴躁,好難討好,尤其係如果有乜嘢嘢打擾佢日間嘅瞓眠。一個溫暖嘅夏日午後,佢喺老橡樹上嘅洞裡打住盹,附近一隻蚱蜢開始唱起一首歡快卻好刺耳嘅歌。老貓頭鷹嘅頭從樹上嗰個既當門又當窗嘅洞口探咗出嚟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 有一隻老貓頭鷹,隨著年紀漸大,變得很暴躁,很難討好,尤其是如果有什麼東西打擾她日間的睡眠。一個溫暖的夏日午後,她在老橡樹上的洞裡打著盹,附近一隻蚱蜢開始唱起一首歡快卻非常刺耳的歌。老貓頭鷹的頭從樹上那個既當門又當窗的洞口探了出來。

passages.original: "Get away from here, sir," she said to the Grasshopper. "Have you no manners? You should at least respect my age and leave me to sleep in quiet!"
passages.vernacular: 「離開呢度,先生,」佢對蚱蜢講。「你冇禮貌嗎?你至少該尊重我嘅年紀,讓我安靜地瞓覺!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「離開這裡,先生,」她對蚱蜢說。「你沒有禮貌嗎?你至少該尊重我的年紀,讓我安靜地睡覺!」

passages.original: But the Grasshopper answered saucily that he had as much right to his place in the sun as the Owl had to her place in the old oak. Then he struck up a louder and still more rasping tune.
passages.vernacular: 但蚱蜢無禮地回答,佢喺陽光下有佢嘅位置,就像貓頭鷹喺老橡樹裡有佢嘅位置一樣有權利。然後佢唱起一首更響亮、更刺耳嘅曲子。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 但蚱蜢無禮地回答,他在陽光下有他的位置,就像貓頭鷹在老橡樹裡有她的位置一樣有權利。然後他唱起一首更響亮、更刺耳的曲子。

passages.original: The wise old Owl knew quite well that it would do no good to argue with the Grasshopper, nor with anybody else for that matter. Besides, her eyes were not sharp enough by day to permit her to punish the Grasshopper as he deserved. So she laid aside all hard words and spoke very kindly to him.
passages.vernacular: 聰明嘅老貓頭鷹好清楚,同蚱蜢爭論係冇用嘅,同其他任何人爭論都係一樣。而且,佢嘅眼睛喺白天唔夠銳利,唔能夠按佢應得嘅懲罰蚱蜢。所以佢放下所有難聽嘅話,好和氣地同佢講話。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 聰明的老貓頭鷹很清楚,同蚱蜢爭論是沒有用的,和其他任何人爭論也是一樣。而且,她的眼睛在白天不夠銳利,不能按他應得的懲罰蚱蜢。所以她放下所有難聽的話,非常和氣地同他說話。

passages.original: "Well sir," she said, "if I must stay awake, I am going to settle right down to enjoy your singing. Now that I think of it, I have a wonderful wine here, sent me from Olympus, of which I am told Apollo drinks before he sings to the high gods. Please come up and taste this delicious drink with me. I know it will make you sing like Apollo himself."
passages.vernacular: 「好吧,先生,」佢講,「如果我必須醒住,我就打算好好坐下嚟欣賞你嘅歌唱。而家想起嚟,我呢度有一種美妙嘅酒,係從奧林匹斯山送畀我嘅,聽講阿波羅喺對眾神歌唱之前飲佢。請上嚟同我一起嘗嘗呢美味嘅飲料。我知道佢會讓你唱得像阿波羅本人一樣。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「好吧,先生,」她說,「如果我必須醒著,我就打算好好坐下來欣賞你的歌唱。現在想起來,我這裡有一種美妙的酒,是從奧林匹斯山送給我的,聽說阿波羅在對眾神歌唱之前喝它。請上來同我一起嘗嘗這美味的飲料。我知道它會讓你唱得像阿波羅本人一樣。」

passages.original: The foolish Grasshopper was taken in by the Owl's flattering words. Up he jumped to the Owl's den, but as soon as he was near enough so the old Owl could see him clearly, she pounced upon him and ate him up.
passages.vernacular: 愚蠢嘅蚱蜢被貓頭鷹嘅奉承話騙喇。佢跳到貓頭鷹嘅洞裡,不過剛一靠近到老貓頭鷹能睇清佢,佢就撲上去,把佢食掉喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 愚蠢的蚱蜢被貓頭鷹的奉承話騙了。他跳到貓頭鷹的洞裡,可是剛一靠近到老貓頭鷹能看清他,她就撲上去,把他吃掉了。

passages.original: Flattery is not a proof of true admiration.
passages.vernacular: 奉承並唔係真誠欽佩嘅證明。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 奉承並不是真誠欽佩的證明。

passages.original: Do not let flattery throw you off your guard against an enemy.
passages.vernacular: 唔好讓奉承使你對敵人放鬆警惕。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不要讓奉承使你對敵人放鬆警惕。

chapters.title: The Wolf and His Shadow 狼與他的影子

passages.original: CH A Wolf left his lair one evening in fine spirits and an excellent appetite. As he ran, the setting sun cast his shadow far out on the ground, and it looked as if the wolf were a hundred times bigger than he really was.
passages.vernacular: 一天傍晚,一隻狼興致勃勃、胃口極好地離開咗佢嘅巢穴。佢奔跑時,夕陽把佢嘅影子投到地上好遠,睇起嚟狼好像比佢實際大咗一百倍。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一天傍晚,一隻狼興致勃勃、胃口極好地離開了他的巢穴。他奔跑時,夕陽把他的影子投到地上很遠,看起來狼好像比他實際大了一百倍。

passages.original: "Why," exclaimed the Wolf proudly, "see how big I am! Fancy me running away from a puny Lion! I'll show him who is fit to be king, he or I."
passages.vernacular: 「瞧,」狼驕傲地喊道,「睇我多大!想想睇我要從一頭弱小嘅獅子面前逃跑!我要讓佢睇睇,到底係佢定係我配當國王。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「瞧,」狼驕傲地喊道,「看我多大!想想看我要從一頭弱小的獅子面前逃跑!我要讓他看看,到底是他還是我配當國王。」

passages.original: Just then an immense shadow blotted him out entirely, and the next instant a Lion struck him down with a single blow.
passages.vernacular: 就喺呢陣,一個巨大嘅影子把佢完全遮住,下一刻一頭獅子一擊就把佢打倒喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 就在這時,一個巨大的影子把他完全遮住,下一刻一頭獅子一擊就把他打倒了。

passages.original: Do not let your fancy make you forget realities.
passages.vernacular: 唔好讓你嘅幻想使你忘記現實。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不要讓你的幻想使你忘記現實。

chapters.title: The Oak and the Reeds 橡樹與蘆葦

passages.original: CH A Giant Oak stood near a brook in which grew some slender Reeds. When the wind blew, the great Oak stood proudly upright with its hundred arms uplifted to the sky. But the Reeds bowed low in the wind and sang a sad and mournful song.
passages.vernacular: 一棵巨大嘅橡樹站喺小溪邊,溪裡長住啲細長嘅蘆葦。風吹嚟時,大橡樹驕傲地挺立住,佢嘅上百條手臂舉向天空。不過蘆葦喺風中深深彎下腰,唱住悲傷哀怨嘅歌。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一棵巨大的橡樹站在小溪邊,溪裡長著一些細長的蘆葦。風吹來時,大橡樹驕傲地挺立著,它的上百條手臂舉向天空。可是蘆葦在風中深深彎下腰,唱著悲傷哀怨的歌。

passages.original: "You have reason to complain," said the Oak. "The slightest breeze that ruffles the surface of the water makes you bow your heads, while I, the mighty Oak, stand upright and firm before the howling tempest."
passages.vernacular: 「你哋有理由抱怨,」橡樹講。「掠過水面嘅最輕微嘅風都讓你哋低下頭,而我,強大嘅橡樹,喺呼嘯嘅暴風雨面前挺立不屈。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你們有理由抱怨,」橡樹說。「掠過水面的最輕微的風都讓你們低下頭,而我,強大的橡樹,在呼嘯的暴風雨面前挺立不屈。」

passages.original: "Do not worry about us," replied the Reeds. "The winds do not harm us. We bow before them and so we do not break. You, in all your pride and strength, have so far resisted their blows. But the end is coming."
passages.vernacular: 「別為我哋擔心,」蘆葦回答。「風傷害不咗我哋。我哋喺佢哋面前彎腰,所以我哋唔會折斷。你,帶住你全部嘅驕傲同力量,迄今抵抗住咗佢哋嘅打擊。但結局就要嚟喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「別為我們擔心,」蘆葦回答。「風傷害不了我們。我們在它們面前彎腰,所以我們不會折斷。你,帶著你全部的驕傲和力量,迄今抵抗住了它們的打擊。但結局就要來了。」

passages.original: As the Reeds spoke a great hurricane rushed out of the north. The Oak stood proudly and fought against the storm, while the yielding Reeds bowed low. The wind redoubled in fury, and all at once the great tree fell, torn up by the roots, and lay among the pitying Reeds.
passages.vernacular: 蘆葦講話時,一陣大颶風從北方衝嚟。橡樹驕傲地站住,同風暴搏鬥,而順從嘅蘆葦深深彎下腰。風嘅狂怒加倍,忽然之間,大樹倒下喇,被連根拔起,躺喺同情佢嘅蘆葦中間。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 蘆葦說話時,一陣大颶風從北方衝來。橡樹驕傲地站著,與風暴搏鬥,而順從的蘆葦深深彎下腰。風的狂怒加倍,忽然之間,大樹倒下了,被連根拔起,躺在同情它的蘆葦中間。

passages.original: Better to yield when it is folly to resist, than to resist stubbornly and be destroyed.
passages.vernacular: 喺抵抗愚蠢時,讓步比頑固抵抗而被毀滅要好。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 在抵抗愚蠢時,讓步比頑固抵抗而被毀滅要好。

chapters.title: The Rat and the Elephant 老鼠與大象

passages.original: CH A Rat was traveling along the King's highway. He was a very proud Rat, considering his small size and the bad reputation all Rats have. As Mr. Rat walked along--he kept mostly to the ditch--he noticed a great commotion up the road, and soon a grand procession came in view. It was the King and his retinue.
passages.vernacular: 一隻老鼠正沿住國王嘅大路旅行。考慮到佢嘅身材矮小,以及所有老鼠嘅壞名聲,佢係一隻好驕傲嘅老鼠。鼠先生走住——佢大部分時間沿住水溝走——佢注意到前面路上一陣大騷動,不久一支盛大嘅隊伍進入視野。嗰個係國王同佢嘅隨從。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻老鼠正沿著國王的大路旅行。考慮到他的身材矮小,以及所有老鼠的壞名聲,他是一隻非常驕傲的老鼠。鼠先生走著——他大部分時間沿著水溝走——他注意到前面路上一陣大騷動,不久一支盛大的隊伍進入視野。那是國王和他的隨從。

passages.original: The King rode on a huge Elephant adorned with the most gorgeous trappings. With the King in his luxurious howdah were the royal Dog and Cat. A great crowd of people followed the procession. They were so taken up with admiration of the Elephant, that the Rat was not noticed. His pride was hurt.
passages.vernacular: 國王騎喺一頭巨大嘅象上,象身上裝飾住最華麗嘅馬飾。同國王一起坐喺佢豪華象轎裡嘅,係皇家嘅狗同貓。一大群人跟喺隊伍後面。佢哋全神貫注地讚歎嗰頭象,冇人注意到老鼠。佢嘅自尊心受傷喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 國王騎在一頭巨大的象上,象身上裝飾著最華麗的馬飾。和國王一起坐在他豪華象轎裡的,是皇家的狗和貓。一大群人跟在隊伍後面。他們全神貫注地讚歎那頭象,沒有人注意到老鼠。他的自尊心受傷了。

passages.original: "What fools!" he cried. "Look at me, and you will soon forget that clumsy Elephant! Is it his great size that makes your eyes pop out? Or is it his wrinkled hide? Why, I have eyes and ears and as many legs as he! I am of just as much importance, and"--
passages.vernacular: 「一群傻瓜!」佢喊道。「睇睇我,你哋好快就會忘記嗰頭笨重嘅象!係佢嘅巨大身材使你哋嘅眼睛都凸出嚟咗嗎?定係佢皺巴巴嘅皮?嗨,我都有眼睛、耳朵,腿同佢一樣多!我嘅重要性同佢一樣,而且——」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「一群傻瓜!」他喊道。「看看我,你們很快就會忘記那頭笨重的象!是他的巨大身材使你們的眼睛都凸出來了嗎?還是他皺巴巴的皮?嗨,我也有眼睛、耳朵,腿和他一樣多!我的重要性和他一樣,而且——」

passages.original: But just then the royal Cat spied him, and the next instant, the Rat knew he was not quite so important as an Elephant.
passages.vernacular: 可就喺呢陣,皇家嘅貓發現咗佢,下一刻,老鼠知道咗佢並不像象嗰樣重要。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 可就在這時,皇家的貓發現了他,下一刻,老鼠知道了他並不像象那樣重要。

passages.original: A resemblance to the great in some things does not make us great.
passages.vernacular: 喺某些方面同偉人相似,並不使我哋偉大。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 在某些方面與偉人相似,並不使我們偉大。

chapters.title: The Boys and the Frogs 男孩們與青蛙

passages.original: CH Some Boys were playing one day at the edge of a pond in which lived a family of Frogs. The Boys amused themselves by throwing stones into the pond so as to make them skip on top of the water.
passages.vernacular: 一天,啲男孩喺一個池塘邊玩耍,池塘裡住一家青蛙。男孩哋以向池塘裡扔石頭取樂,讓石頭喺水面上跳躍。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一天,一些男孩在一個池塘邊玩耍,池塘裡住著一家青蛙。男孩們以向池塘裡扔石頭取樂,讓石頭在水面上跳躍。

passages.original: The stones were flying thick and fast and the Boys were enjoying themselves very much; but the poor Frogs in the pond were trembling with fear.
passages.vernacular: 石頭又密又快地飛住,男孩哋玩得好開心;不過池塘裡可憐嘅青蛙哋嚇得渾身發抖。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 石頭又密又快地飛著,男孩們玩得很開心;可是池塘裡可憐的青蛙們嚇得渾身發抖。

passages.original: At last one of the Frogs, the oldest and bravest, put his head out of the water, and said, "Oh, please, dear children, stop your cruel play! Though it may be fun for you, it means death to us!"
passages.vernacular: 最後,其中最老、最勇敢嘅一隻青蛙把頭探出水面,講:「哦,親愛嘅細路哋,請停止你哋殘忍嘅遊戲吧!雖然對你哋來講可能好玩,對我哋卻意味住死亡!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 最後,其中最老、最勇敢的一隻青蛙把頭探出水面,說:「哦,親愛的孩子們,請停止你們殘忍的遊戲吧!雖然對你們來說可能好玩,對我們卻意味著死亡!」

passages.original: Always stop to think whether your fun may not be the cause of another's unhappiness.
passages.vernacular: 總要停下嚟想一想,你嘅樂趣係咪可能成為別人不幸嘅原因。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 總要停下來想一想,你的樂趣是否可能成為別人不幸的原因。

chapters.title: The Crow and the Pitcher 烏鴉與水罐

passages.original: CH In a spell of dry weather, when the Birds could find very little to drink, a thirsty Crow found a pitcher with a little water in it. But the pitcher was high and had a narrow neck, and no matter how he tried, the Crow could not reach the water. The poor thing felt as if he must die of thirst.
passages.vernacular: 喺一段乾旱嘅天氣裡,鳥兒哋找唔到乜嘢水飲,一隻口渴嘅烏鴉發現一個罐子裡有啲水。不過罐子好高,脖子又窄,不管佢點樣努力,烏鴉都夠唔到水。可憐嘅傢伙覺得自己一定會渴死。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 在一段乾旱的天氣裡,鳥兒們找不到什麼水喝,一隻口渴的烏鴉發現一個罐子裡有一點水。可是罐子很高,脖子又窄,不管他怎樣努力,烏鴉都夠不到水。可憐的傢伙覺得自己一定會渴死。

passages.original: Then an idea came to him. Picking up some small pebbles, he dropped them into the pitcher one by one. With each pebble the water rose a little higher until at last it was near enough so he could drink.
passages.vernacular: 然後佢想到咗一個主意。佢撿起啲小石子,一顆一顆地扔進罐子裡。每放一顆石子,水就升高啲,最後升到夠近嘅地方,佢就能飲到喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後他想到了一個主意。他撿起一些小石子,一顆一顆地扔進罐子裡。每放一顆石子,水就升高一點,最後升到夠近的地方,他就能喝到了。

passages.original: In a pinch a good use of our wits may help us out.
passages.vernacular: 喺緊要關頭,好好運用我哋嘅智慧,可以幫我哋解圍。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 在緊要關頭,好好運用我們的智慧,可以幫我們解圍。

chapters.title: The Ants and the Grasshopper 螞蟻與蚱蜢

passages.original: CH One bright day in late autumn a family of Ants were bustling about in the warm sunshine, drying out the grain they had stored up during the summer, when a starving Grasshopper, his fiddle under his arm, came up and humbly begged for a bite to eat.
passages.vernacular: 晚秋裡一個晴朗嘅日子,一家螞蟻正在溫暖嘅陽光下忙忙碌碌,曬住佢哋夏天儲存起嚟嘅穀物,呢陣一隻快要餓死嘅蚱蜢,把小提琴夾喺胳膊下面,走過嚟謙卑地乞求一口食嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 晚秋裡一個晴朗的日子,一家螞蟻正在溫暖的陽光下忙忙碌碌,曬著他們夏天儲存起來的穀物,這時一隻快要餓死的蚱蜢,把小提琴夾在胳膊下面,走過來謙卑地乞求一口吃的。

passages.original: "What!" cried the Ants in surprise, "haven't you stored anything away for the winter? What in the world were you doing all last summer?"
passages.vernacular: 「乜嘢!」螞蟻哋驚訝地喊道,「你冇為冬天儲存任何嘢嗎?去年整個夏天你到底喺幹乜嘢?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「什麼!」螞蟻們驚訝地喊道,「你沒有為冬天儲存任何東西嗎?去年整個夏天你到底在幹什麼?」

passages.original: "I didn't have time to store up any food," whined the Grasshopper; "I was so busy making music that before I knew it the summer was gone."
passages.vernacular: 「我冇時間儲存食物,」蚱蜢哭訴道;「我忙住演奏音樂,唔知不覺夏天就過去喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我沒有時間儲存食物,」蚱蜢哭訴道;「我忙著演奏音樂,不知不覺夏天就過去了。」

passages.original: The Ants shrugged their shoulders in disgust.
passages.vernacular: 螞蟻哋厭惡地聳聳肩。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 螞蟻們厭惡地聳聳肩。

passages.original: "Making music, were you?" they cried. "Very well; now dance!" And they turned their backs on the Grasshopper and went on with their work.
passages.vernacular: 「你喺演奏音樂,係嗎?」佢哋喊道。「好好,而家跳舞吧!」講完佢哋背過身去,不理蚱蜢,繼續幹活。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你在演奏音樂,是嗎?」他們喊道。「很好,現在跳舞吧!」說完他們背過身去,不理蚱蜢,繼續幹活。

passages.original: There's a time for work and a time for play.
passages.vernacular: 工作有工作嘅時候,玩樂有玩樂嘅時候。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 工作有工作的時候,玩樂有玩樂的時候。

chapters.title: The Ass Carrying the Image 馱神像的驢子

passages.original: CH A sacred Image was being carried to the temple. It was mounted on an Ass adorned with garlands and gorgeous trappings, and a grand procession of priests and pages followed it through the streets. As the Ass walked along, the people bowed their heads reverently or fell on their knees, and the Ass thought the honor was being paid to himself.
passages.vernacular: 一尊神聖嘅神像正被抬往神廟。佢安放喺一頭驢子身上,驢子身上裝飾住花環同華麗嘅馬飾,一支盛大嘅祭司同侍從隊伍跟喺後面穿過街道。驢子走住,人哋恭敬地低頭或跪倒,驢子以為呢份榮耀係畀佢自己嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一尊神聖的神像正被抬往神廟。它安放在一頭驢子身上,驢子身上裝飾著花環和華麗的馬飾,一支盛大的祭司和侍從隊伍跟在後面穿過街道。驢子走著,人們恭敬地低頭或跪倒,驢子以為這份榮耀是給他自己的。

passages.original: With his head full of this foolish idea, he became so puffed up with pride and vanity that he halted and started to bray loudly. But in the midst of his song, his driver guessed what the Ass had got into his head, and began to beat him unmercifully with a stick.
passages.vernacular: 腦子裡裝滿咗呢個愚蠢嘅念頭,佢得意洋洋,驕傲自大,停下嚟開始大聲嘶叫。但喺佢歌唱嘅當口,佢嘅趕驢人猜到咗驢子腦子裡想嘅係乜嘢,開始用棍子無情地打佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 腦子裡裝滿了這個愚蠢的念頭,他得意洋洋,驕傲自大,停下來開始大聲嘶叫。但在他歌唱的當口,他的趕驢人猜到了驢子腦子裡想的是什麼,開始用棍子無情地打他。

passages.original: "Go along with you, you stupid Ass," he cried. "The honor is not meant for you but for the image you are carrying."
passages.vernacular: 「走吧你,你呢蠢驢,」佢喊道。「呢榮耀唔係畀你嘅,而係畀你背嘅神像嘅。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「走吧你,你這蠢驢,」他喊道。「這榮耀不是給你的,而是給你背的神像的。」

passages.original: Do not try to take the credit to yourself that is due to others.
passages.vernacular: 唔好試圖把應屬於別人嘅功勞據為己有。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不要試圖把應屬於別人的功勞據為己有。

chapters.title: A Raven and a Swan 烏鴉與天鵝

passages.original: CH A Raven, which you know is black as coal, was envious of the Swan, because her feathers were as white as the purest snow. The foolish bird got the idea that if he lived like the Swan, swimming and diving all day long and eating the weeds and plants that grow in the water, his feathers would turn white like the Swan's.
passages.vernacular: 一隻烏鴉,你知道,係黑得像煤炭嘅,佢嫉妒天鵝,因為佢嘅羽毛像最純淨嘅雪一樣白。呢隻愚蠢嘅鳥冒出一個想法:如果佢像天鵝嗰樣生活,整天游泳、潛水,食水中生長嘅水草同植物,佢嘅羽毛就會變得像天鵝嘅一樣白。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻烏鴉,你知道,是黑得像煤炭的,他嫉妒天鵝,因為她的羽毛像最純淨的雪一樣白。這隻愚蠢的鳥冒出一個想法:如果他像天鵝那樣生活,整天游泳、潛水,吃水中生長的水草和植物,他的羽毛就會變得像天鵝的一樣白。

passages.original: So he left his home in the woods and fields and flew down to live on the lakes and in the marshes. But though he washed and washed all day long, almost drowning himself at it, his feathers remained as black as ever. And as the water weeds he ate did not agree with him, he got thinner and thinner, and at last he died.
passages.vernacular: 於是佢離開咗喺樹林同田野裡嘅家,飛下嚟住喺湖上同沼澤裡。不過儘管佢整天洗咗又洗,幾乎把自己淹死,佢嘅羽毛定係同以前一樣黑。而且因為佢食嘅水草不適合佢,佢越嚟越瘦,最後死喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 於是他離開了在樹林和田野裡的家,飛下來住在湖上和沼澤裡。可是儘管他整天洗了又洗,幾乎把自己淹死,他的羽毛還是和以前一樣黑。而且因為他吃的水草不適合他,他越來越瘦,最後死了。

passages.original: A change of habits will not alter nature.
passages.vernacular: 改變習慣唔會改變本性。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 改變習慣不會改變本性。

chapters.title: The Two Goats 兩隻山羊

passages.original: CH Two Goats, frisking gayly on the rocky steeps of a mountain valley, chanced to meet, one on each side of a deep chasm through which poured a mighty mountain torrent. The trunk of a fallen tree formed the only means of crossing the chasm, and on this not even two squirrels could have passed each other in safety. The narrow path would have made the bravest tremble. Not so our Goats. Their pride would not permit either to stand aside for the other.
passages.vernacular: 兩隻山羊喺山谷中險峻嘅岩石上快活地蹦跳,碰巧喺一條深澗嘅兩側相遇,澗中奔流住洶湧嘅山洪。一根倒下嘅樹幹係越過深澗嘅唯一方法,喺上面,即使兩隻松鼠都唔能夠安全地擦身而過。呢條窄路會讓最勇敢嘅人都發抖。我哋嘅山羊卻不然。佢哋嘅驕傲使佢哋邊個都唔肯畀對方讓路。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 兩隻山羊在山谷中險峻的岩石上快活地蹦跳,碰巧在一條深澗的兩側相遇,澗中奔流著洶湧的山洪。一根倒下的樹幹是越過深澗的唯一方法,在上面,即使兩隻松鼠也不能安全地擦身而過。這條窄路會讓最勇敢的人也發抖。我們的山羊卻不然。她們的驕傲使她們誰也不肯給對方讓路。

passages.original: One set her foot on the log. The other did likewise. In the middle they met horn to horn. Neither would give way, and so they both fell, to be swept away by the roaring torrent below.
passages.vernacular: 一隻把腳踩喺原木上。另一隻都一樣。喺中間,佢哋角對角相遇喇。邊個都唔肯讓步,於是佢哋都掉咗下去,被下面咆哮嘅洪流沖走喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻把腳踩在原木上。另一隻也一樣。在中間,她們角對角相遇了。誰也不肯讓步,於是她們都掉了下去,被下面咆哮的洪流沖走了。

passages.original: It is better to yield than to come to misfortune through stubbornness.
passages.vernacular: 讓步勝過因固執而招致不幸。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 讓步勝過因固執而招致不幸。

chapters.title: The Ass and the Load of Salt 驢子與一袋鹽

passages.original: CH A Merchant, driving his Ass homeward from the seashore with a heavy load of salt, came to a river crossed by a shallow ford. They had crossed this river many times before without accident, but this time the Ass slipped and fell when halfway over. And when the Merchant at last got him to his feet, much of the salt had melted away. Delighted to find how much lighter his burden had become, the Ass finished the journey very gayly.
passages.vernacular: 一個商人趕住佢嘅驢子,馱住一大袋沉重嘅鹽從海邊回家,嚟到一條有淺灘可涉嘅河邊。佢哋以前多次過呢條河都平安無事,但呢次驢子走到一半滑倒喇。當商人終於把佢拉起嚟時,大部分嘅鹽都已經融化掉喇。驢子發現佢嘅負擔輕咗咁多,高興極喇,好快活地走完咗剩下嘅旅程。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一個商人趕著他的驢子,馱著一大袋沉重的鹽從海邊回家,來到一條有淺灘可涉的河邊。他們以前多次過這條河都平安無事,但這次驢子走到一半滑倒了。當商人終於把他拉起來時,大部分的鹽都已經融化掉了。驢子發現他的負擔輕了這麼多,高興極了,非常快活地走完了剩下的旅程。

passages.original: Next day the Merchant went for another load of salt. On the way home the Ass, remembering what had happened at the ford, purposely let himself fall into the water, and again got rid of most of his burden.
passages.vernacular: 第二天,商人又去運另一批鹽。回家嘅路上,驢子想起淺灘上發生嘅事,故意讓自己跌進水裡,又擺脫咗大部分嘅負擔。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 第二天,商人又去運另一批鹽。回家的路上,驢子想起淺灘上發生的事,故意讓自己跌進水裡,又擺脫了大部分的負擔。

passages.original: The angry Merchant immediately turned about and drove the Ass back to the seashore, where he loaded him with two great baskets of sponges. At the ford the Ass again tumbled over; but when he had scrambled to his feet, it was a very disconsolate Ass that dragged himself homeward under a load ten times heavier than before.
passages.vernacular: 生氣嘅商人即刻掉頭,把驢子趕回海邊,喺嗰度佢畀佢裝上咗兩大筐海綿。喺淺灘,驢子又摔倒喇;但當佢爬起嚟時,嗰個係一頭好沮喪嘅驢子,拖住比以前重十倍嘅負擔走回家。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 生氣的商人立刻掉頭,把驢子趕回海邊,在那裡他給他裝上了兩大筐海綿。在淺灘,驢子又摔倒了;但當他爬起來時,那是一頭非常沮喪的驢子,拖著比以前重十倍的負擔走回家。

passages.original: The same measures will not suit all circumstances.
passages.vernacular: 同樣嘅辦法唔能夠適用於所有情況。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 同樣的辦法不能適用於所有情況。

chapters.title: The Lion and the Gnat 獅子與蚊蟲

passages.original: CH "Away with you, vile insect!" said a Lion angrily to a Gnat that was buzzing around his head. But the Gnat was not in the least disturbed.
passages.vernacular: 「滾開,可惡嘅蟲子!」一頭獅子生氣地對喺佢頭周圍嗡嗡叫嘅蚊蟲講。不過蚊蟲啲都冇被嚇到。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「滾開,可惡的蟲子!」一頭獅子生氣地對在他頭周圍嗡嗡叫的蚊蟲說。可是蚊蟲一點也沒被嚇到。

passages.original: "Do you think," he said spitefully to the Lion, "that I am afraid of you because they call you king?"
passages.vernacular: 「你以為,」佢惡意地對獅子講,「因為人家叫你國王,我就怕你嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你以為,」他惡意地對獅子說,「因為人家叫你國王,我就怕你嗎?」

passages.original: The next instant he flew at the Lion and stung him sharply on the nose. Mad with rage, the Lion struck fiercely at the Gnat, but only succeeded in tearing himself with his claws. Again and again the Gnat stung the Lion, who now was roaring terribly. At last, worn out with rage and covered with wounds that his own teeth and claws had made, the Lion gave up the fight.
passages.vernacular: 下一刻佢飛向獅子,尖銳地叮咗佢嘅鼻子一下。獅子氣瘋喇,猛力撲打蚊蟲,卻只係用爪子抓傷咗自己。蚊蟲一次又一次地叮獅子,獅子而家吼得可怕。最後,獅子氣得筋疲力盡,身上滿係佢自己嘅牙齒同爪子造成嘅傷口,放棄咗戰鬥。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 下一刻他飛向獅子,尖銳地叮了他的鼻子一下。獅子氣瘋了,猛力撲打蚊蟲,卻只是用爪子抓傷了自己。蚊蟲一次又一次地叮獅子,獅子現在吼得可怕。最後,獅子氣得筋疲力盡,身上滿是他自己的牙齒和爪子造成的傷口,放棄了戰鬥。

passages.original: The Gnat buzzed away to tell the whole world about his victory, but instead he flew straight into a spider's web. And there, he who had defeated the King of beasts came to a miserable end, the prey of a little spider.
passages.vernacular: 蚊蟲嗡嗡地飛走,要把佢嘅勝利告訴全世界,不過佢卻直接飛進咗蜘蛛網。就咁樣,嗰個擊敗咗百獸之王嘅,可悲地死喇,成咗一隻小蜘蛛嘅獵物。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 蚊蟲嗡嗡地飛走,要把他的勝利告訴全世界,可是他卻直接飛進了蜘蛛網。就這樣,那個擊敗了百獸之王的,可悲地死了,成了一隻小蜘蛛的獵物。

passages.original: The least of our enemies is often the most to be feared.
passages.vernacular: 我哋最小嘅敵人,往往最值得害怕。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們最小的敵人,往往最值得害怕。

passages.original: Pride over a success should not throw us off our guard.
passages.vernacular: 因成功而生嘅驕傲,唔應該該讓我哋放鬆警惕。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 因成功而生的驕傲,不應該讓我們放鬆警惕。

chapters.title: The Leap at Rhodes 羅德島的一跳

passages.original: CH A certain man who visited foreign lands could talk of little when he returned to his home except the wonderful adventures he had met with and the great deeds he had done abroad.
passages.vernacular: 一個到過外國嘅人,回家後除咗談佢遇到嘅奇妙冒險同喺國外做嘅偉大事蹟之外,幾乎冇別嘅可講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一個到過外國的人,回家後除了談他遇到的奇妙冒險和在國外做的偉大事蹟之外,幾乎沒有別的可說。

passages.original: One of the feats he told about was a leap he had made in a city Called Rhodes. That leap was so great, he said, that no other man could leap anywhere near the distance. A great many persons in Rhodes had seen him do it and would prove that what he told was true.
passages.vernacular: 佢講嘅豐功偉績之一,係佢喺一座叫羅德島嘅城市裡做嘅一次跳躍。佢講,嗰一跳好了不起,冇別人能跳到接近嗰個距離。羅德島嘅許多人都見佢跳過,可以證明佢講嘅係真嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他講的豐功偉績之一,是他在一座叫羅德島的城市裡做的一次跳躍。他說,那一跳非常了不起,沒有別人能跳到接近那個距離。羅德島的許多人都見他跳過,可以證明他說的是真的。

passages.original: "No need of witnesses," said one of the hearers. "Suppose this city is Rhodes. Now show us how far you can jump."
passages.vernacular: 「不需要證人,」一個聽嘅人講。「假設呢座城市就係羅德島。而家讓我哋睇睇你能跳多遠。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「不需要證人,」一個聽的人說。「假設這座城市就是羅德島。現在讓我們看看你能跳多遠。」

passages.original: Deeds count, not boasting words.
passages.vernacular: 行動算數,誇誇其談不算數。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 行動算數,誇誇其談不算數。

chapters.title: The Cock and the Jewel 公雞與寶石

passages.original: CH A Cock was busily scratching and scraping about to find something to eat for himself and his family, when he happened to turn up a precious jewel that had been lost by its owner.
passages.vernacular: 一隻公雞正忙住呢兒刨、嗰兒扒,為自己同家人找食嘅,碰巧刨出一顆被主人丟失嘅珍貴寶石。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一隻公雞正忙著這兒刨、那兒扒,為自己和家人找吃的,碰巧刨出一顆被主人丟失的珍貴寶石。

passages.original: "Aha!" said the Cock. "No doubt you are very costly and he who lost you would give a great deal to find you. But as for me, I would choose a single grain of barleycorn before all the jewels in the world."
passages.vernacular: 「哈!」公雞講。「無疑你好值錢,丟咗你嘅人會花好大代價嚟找你。但就我來講,我寧願要一粒大麥,都唔好世上所有嘅寶石。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「哈!」公雞說。「無疑你很值錢,丟了你的人會花很大代價來找你。但就我來說,我寧願要一粒大麥,也不要世上所有的寶石。」

passages.original: Precious things are without value to those who cannot prize them.
passages.vernacular: 對不懂得珍視嘅人來講,珍貴嘅嘢係冇價值嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 對不懂得珍視的人來說,珍貴的東西是沒有價值的。

chapters.title: The Monkey and the Camel 猴子與駱駝

passages.original: CH At a great celebration in honor of King Lion, the Monkey was asked to dance for the company. His dancing was very clever indeed, and the animals were all highly pleased with his grace and lightness.
passages.vernacular: 喺為獅子國王舉行嘅一次盛大慶典上,猴子被邀請為大家跳舞。佢嘅舞跳得確實好機靈,動物哋都對佢嘅優雅輕盈好滿意。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 在為獅子國王舉行的一次盛大慶典上,猴子被邀請為大家跳舞。他的舞跳得確實很機靈,動物們都對他的優雅輕盈非常滿意。

passages.original: The praise that was showered on the Monkey made the Camel envious. He was very sure that he could dance quite as well as the Monkey, if not better, so he pushed his way into the crowd that was gathered around the Monkey, and rising on his hind legs, began to dance. But the big hulking Camel made himself very ridiculous as he kicked out his knotty legs and twisted his long clumsy neck. Besides, the animals found it hard to keep their toes from under his heavy hoofs.
passages.vernacular: 大家對猴子嘅一片讚美使駱駝嫉妒。佢好肯定自己跳得同猴子一樣好,如果唔係更好嘅話,於是佢擠進圍住猴子嘅人群,用後腿站起嚟,開始跳舞。但係呢頭又高又笨重嘅駱駝踢住佢疙疙瘩瘩嘅腿、扭住佢又長又笨拙嘅脖子,樣子好可笑。而且動物哋發現,好難讓腳趾躲開佢沉重嘅蹄子。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 大家對猴子的一片讚美使駱駝嫉妒。他很肯定自己跳得和猴子一樣好,如果不是更好的話,於是他擠進圍著猴子的人群,用後腿站起來,開始跳舞。但是這頭又高又笨重的駱駝踢著他疙疙瘩瘩的腿、扭著他又長又笨拙的脖子,樣子非常可笑。而且動物們發現,很難讓腳趾躲開他沉重的蹄子。

passages.original: At last, when one of his huge feet came within an inch of King Lion's nose, the animals were so disgusted that they set upon the Camel in a rage and drove him out into the desert.
passages.vernacular: 最後,當佢嘅一隻大腳離獅子國王嘅鼻子只有一英寸時,動物哋厭惡極喇,憤怒地撲向駱駝,把佢趕進咗沙漠。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 最後,當他的一隻大腳離獅子國王的鼻子只有一英寸時,動物們厭惡極了,憤怒地撲向駱駝,把他趕進了沙漠。

passages.original: Shortly afterward, refreshments, consisting mostly of Camel's hump and ribs, were served to the company.
passages.vernacular: 不久之後,點心端畀咗大家,主要係駱駝嘅駝峰同肋骨。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不久之後,點心端給了大家,主要是駱駝的駝峰和肋骨。

passages.original: Do not try to ape your betters.
passages.vernacular: 唔好試圖模仿比你強嘅人。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不要試圖模仿比你強的人。

chapters.title: The Wild Boar and the Fox 野豬與狐狸

passages.original: CH A Wild Boar was sharpening his tusks busily against the stump of a tree, when a Fox happened by. Now the Fox was always looking for a chance to make fun of his neighbors. So he made a great show of looking anxiously about, as if in fear of some hidden enemy. But the Boar kept right on with his work.
passages.vernacular: 一頭野豬正忙住喺樹樁上磨佢嘅獠牙,一隻狐狸碰巧經過。嗰隻狐狸總是喺尋找機會取笑佢嘅鄰居。所以佢裝模作樣地焦急四顧,好像怕有乜嘢隱藏嘅敵人。但野豬繼續幹佢嘅活。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一頭野豬正忙著在樹樁上磨他的獠牙,一隻狐狸碰巧經過。那隻狐狸總是在尋找機會取笑他的鄰居。所以他裝模作樣地焦急四顧,好像怕有什麼隱藏的敵人。但野豬繼續幹他的活。

passages.original: "Why are you doing that?" asked the Fox at last with a grin. "There isn't any danger that I can see."
passages.vernacular: 「你點解嗰樣做?」狐狸終於咧住嘴問。「據我所見,冇任何危險。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你為什麼那樣做?」狐狸終於咧著嘴問。「據我所見,沒有任何危險。」

passages.original: "True enough," replied the Boar, "but when danger does come there will not be time for such work as this. My weapons will have to be ready for use then, or I shall suffer for it."
passages.vernacular: 「確實,」野豬回答,「不過危險真嘅嚟喇,就冇時間做呢種活喇。到嗰時我嘅武器必須準備好可以使用,否則我就要食苦頭喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「確實,」野豬回答,「可是危險真的來了,就沒有時間做這種活了。到那時我的武器必須準備好可以使用,否則我就要吃苦頭了。」

passages.original: Preparedness for war is the best guarantee of peace.
passages.vernacular: 戰備係和平嘅最佳保證。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 戰備是和平的最佳保證。

chapters.title: The Ass, the Fox, and the Lion 驢子、狐狸與獅子

passages.original: CH An Ass and a Fox had become close comrades, and were constantly in each other's company. While the Ass cropped a fresh bit of greens, the Fox would devour a chicken from the neighboring farmyard or a bit of cheese filched from the dairy. One day the pair unexpectedly met a Lion. The Ass was very much frightened, but the Fox calmed his fears.
passages.vernacular: 一頭驢子同一隻狐狸成咗密友,總是形影不離。驢子啃啲新鮮嘅青草時,狐狸就食鄰近農場嘅一隻雞或從乳品房偷嚟嘅啲乳酪。有一天,呢一對意外地遇見咗一頭獅子。驢子好害怕,但狐狸安撫咗佢嘅恐懼。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一頭驢子和一隻狐狸成了密友,總是形影不離。驢子啃一點新鮮的青草時,狐狸就吃鄰近農場的一隻雞或從乳品房偷來的一點乳酪。有一天,這一對意外地遇見了一頭獅子。驢子非常害怕,但狐狸安撫了他的恐懼。

passages.original: "I will talk to him," he said.
passages.vernacular: 「我去同佢講,」佢講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我去同他說,」他說。

passages.original: So the Fox walked boldly up to the Lion.
passages.vernacular: 於是狐狸大膽地走到獅子面前。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 於是狐狸大膽地走到獅子面前。

passages.original: "Your highness," he said in an undertone, so the Ass could not hear him, "I've got a fine scheme in my head. If you promise not to hurt me, I will lead that foolish creature yonder into a pit where he can't get out, and you can feast at your pleasure."
passages.vernacular: 「殿下,」佢低聲講,不讓驢子聽見,「我有一個好計劃。如果你答應不傷害我,我就把嗰邊嗰個蠢傢伙引進一個佢出不嚟嘅坑裡,你可以隨意享用。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「殿下,」他低聲說,不讓驢子聽見,「我有一個好計劃。如果你答應不傷害我,我就把那邊那個蠢傢伙引進一個他出不來的坑裡,你可以隨意享用。」

passages.original: The Lion agreed and the Fox returned to the Ass.
passages.vernacular: 獅子同意喇,狐狸回到驢子身邊。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 獅子同意了,狐狸回到驢子身邊。

passages.original: "I made him promise not to hurt us," said the Fox. "But come, I know a good place to hide till he is gone."
passages.vernacular: 「我讓佢答應不傷害我哋,」狐狸講。「嚟吧,我知道一個好地方可以躲到佢走。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我讓他答應不傷害我們,」狐狸說。「來吧,我知道一個好地方可以躲到他走。」

passages.original: So the Fox led the Ass into a deep pit. But when the Lion saw that the Ass was his for the taking, he first of all struck down the traitor Fox.
passages.vernacular: 於是狐狸把驢子領進一個深坑。但獅子睇到驢子已經手到擒嚟,首先打倒嘅卻係叛徒狐狸。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 於是狐狸把驢子領進一個深坑。但獅子看到驢子已經手到擒來,首先打倒的卻是叛徒狐狸。

passages.original: Traitors may expect treachery.
passages.vernacular: 叛徒可以預料會遭到背叛。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 叛徒可以預料會遭到背叛。

chapters.title: The Birds, the Beasts, and the Bat 鳥、獸與蝙蝠

passages.original: CH The Birds and the Beasts declared war against each other. No compromise was possible, and so they went at it tooth and claw. It is said the quarrel grew out of the persecution the race of Geese suffered at the teeth of the Fox family. The Beasts, too, had cause for fight. The Eagle was constantly pouncing on the Hare, and the Owl dined daily on Mice.
passages.vernacular: 鳥類同獸類互相宣戰。冇任何妥協嘅可能,於是佢哋用牙齒同爪子打咗起嚟。據講呢場爭吵係因為鵝呢個種族遭到狐狸家族嘅牙齒迫害而起嘅。獸類都有開戰嘅理由。老鷹不斷撲向野兔,貓頭鷹每天以老鼠為食。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 鳥類和獸類互相宣戰。沒有任何妥協的可能,於是他們用牙齒和爪子打了起來。據說這場爭吵是因為鵝這個種族遭到狐狸家族的牙齒迫害而起的。獸類也有開戰的理由。老鷹不斷撲向野兔,貓頭鷹每天以老鼠為食。

passages.original: It was a terrible battle. Many a Hare and many a Mouse died. Chickens and Geese fell by the score--and the victor always stopped for a feast.
passages.vernacular: 呢個係一場可怕嘅戰鬥。許多野兔同許多老鼠死去。雞同鵝成打地倒下——勝利者總要停下嚟大食一頓。
